name: General Knowledge

questions.question: In which year did the Battle of Hastings take place?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Hastings took place on October 14, 1066, leading to the Norman conquest of England by William the Conqueror.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other dates are: 1215 (signing of Magna Carta), 1492 (Columbus reached the Americas), and 1099 (capture of Jerusalem in the First Crusade).

questions.question: Which Roman emperor was legendarily said to have fiddled while Rome burned in 64 AD?
questions.explanation_correct: Ancient historians (like Tacitus) accused Nero of initiating the Great Fire of Rome in order to build his massive Golden House (Domus Aurea).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Julius Caesar was a dictator, not an emperor. Augustus was the first emperor. Caligula was notorious but died before the fire.

questions.question: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall, symbolising the end of the Cold War in Europe?
questions.explanation_correct: The Berlin Wall was opened on November 9, 1989, leading to the collapse of East German communist rule and the subsequent reunification of Germany.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1991 was the dissolution of the Soviet Union, 1985 was Gorbachev's ascension to power, and 1993 was the dissolution of Czechoslovakia.

questions.question: In which year did the Battle of Marathon take place?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Marathon took place in 490 BC, where the Athenians defeated the Persian invasion force led by Darius I.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 480 BC was the Battle of Thermopylae, 431 BC was the start of the Peloponnesian War, and 338 BC was the Battle of Chaeronea.

questions.question: In which year did the United States enter World War II following the attack on Pearl Harbor?
questions.explanation_correct: The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor occurred on December 7, 1941, prompting the US to declare war the following day.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1939 was when WWII started in Europe, 1940 was the Battle of Britain, and 1942 was the Battle of Midway.

questions.question: Which royal fortress and prison was stormed on July 14, 1789, marking the start of the French Revolution?
questions.explanation_correct: The storming of the Bastille became a symbol of the uprising against the absolute monarchy of Louis XVI.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Conciergerie was another prison, Château d'If is near Marseille, and Versailles was the royal residence.

questions.question: Who was the first President of the United States, inaugurated in 1789?
questions.explanation_correct: George Washington served as Commander-in-Chief during the Revolutionary War and became the first president under the US Constitution.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adams and Jefferson were the 2nd and 3rd presidents. Franklin was a founding father but never president.

questions.question: In which year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Caribbean, launching transatlantic contact?
questions.explanation_correct: Columbus reached the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, sailing under the Spanish flag.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1488 was when Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope. The others were later voyages of Columbus.

questions.question: Which city was the site of the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914, triggering World War I?
questions.explanation_correct: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip on June 28, 1914.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Belgrade was the capital of Serbia. Vienna and Budapest were the capital cities of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

questions.question: Who discovered the intact tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922?
questions.explanation_correct: British archaeologist Howard Carter discovered the tomb (KV62) in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Schliemann excavated Troy, Evans discovered Knossos on Crete, and Champollion deciphered the Rosetta Stone.

questions.question: Which English king was forced by his barons to sign the Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.explanation_correct: King John signed the Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215, establishing the principle that everyone, including the king, is subject to the law.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Richard I was John's brother and predecessor. Henry II was their father. Edward I ruled later in the 13th century.

questions.question: In which year did the Cuban Missile Crisis bring the world to the brink of nuclear war?
questions.explanation_correct: The confrontation between the US and the USSR over Soviet missiles in Cuba occurred in October 1962.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1961 was the Bay of Pigs invasion, 1963 was the JFK assassination, and 1959 was the Cuban Revolution.

questions.question: In which year did Neil Armstrong become the first human to walk on the Moon?
questions.explanation_correct: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, and Neil Armstrong took his historic first steps shortly after.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1961 was Yuri Gagarin's flight. 1972 was the last Apollo moonwalk (Apollo 17). 1965 was the first US spacewalk.

questions.question: On which date (known as the Ides of March) was Julius Caesar assassinated in 44 BC?
questions.explanation_correct: Julius Caesar was stabbed to death by a group of senators, including Brutus and Cassius, on March 15, 44 BC.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other dates are simply close calendar days.

questions.question: In which battle was Napoleon Bonaparte finally defeated in 1815, ending the Napoleonic Wars?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Waterloo (June 18, 1815) in present-day Belgium resulted in Napoleon's final abdication.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Leipzig (1813) was a major defeat but not the end. Austerlitz (1805) was Napoleon's greatest victory. Borodino (1812) was in Russia.

questions.question: In which year did the October Revolution occur in Russia, leading to the rise of the Soviet Union?
questions.explanation_correct: The October Revolution, led by Lenin and the Bolsheviks, took place in November 1917 (October in the Julian calendar).
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1905 was the first Russian revolution, 1914 was the start of WWI, and 1922 was the formal creation of the USSR.

questions.question: How many years did the conflict known as the 'Hundred Years' War' actually last?
questions.explanation_correct: The war between the houses of Valois and Plantagenet lasted from 1337 to 1453, which is 116 years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 100 is the name of the war but not its exact length.

questions.question: In which year did the American Civil War begin?
questions.explanation_correct: The Civil War began in April 1861 when Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter in South Carolina.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1865 was the year the war ended. 1860 was Lincoln's election. 1859 was John Brown's raid.

questions.question: Which volcano erupted in 79 AD, destroying the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum?
questions.explanation_correct: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, burying the Roman settlements under layers of ash and pumice.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Etna is in Sicily, while Stromboli and Vulcano are active Aeolian island volcanoes.

questions.question: In which year did the Titanic sink after striking an iceberg in the North Atlantic?
questions.explanation_correct: The Titanic sank on April 15, 1912, during its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1914 was the start of WWI. 1908 and 1910 were years of Titanic's design and early construction.

questions.question: Which Carthaginian general led an army, including war elephants, across the Alps to attack Rome?
questions.explanation_correct: Hannibal Barca crossed the Alps in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scipio was his Roman rival. Hamilcar was his father. Caesar was a Roman general centuries later.

questions.question: In which year was Charlemagne crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III?
questions.explanation_correct: Charlemagne was crowned on Christmas Day in the year 800 in St. Peter's Basilica, Rome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 962 was the coronation of Otto I (Holy Roman Emperor), 1066 was the Norman Conquest, and 753 BC is the legendary founding of Rome.

questions.question: In which year did World War I officially end with the signing of the armistice?
questions.explanation_correct: The armistice went into effect at 11:00 AM on November 11, 1918.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1919 was when the Treaty of Versailles was signed. 1917 was when the US entered the war.

questions.question: Which alliance of Western nations was established in 1949 to provide collective security against the Soviet Union?
questions.explanation_correct: NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was signed in Washington, D.C., in April 1949.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Warsaw Pact was the Soviet response (1955). The UN (1945) and League of Nations (1920) were global bodies.

questions.question: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal as a mausoleum for his favorite wife Mumtaz Mahal?
questions.explanation_correct: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal in Agra around 1632.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Babur founded the Mughal empire. Akbar was the greatest Mughal ruler. Aurangzeb was Shah Jahan's son and successor.

questions.question: In which year did the United States declare independence from Great Britain?
questions.explanation_correct: The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1783 was the end of the Revolutionary War. 1789 was the start of the Constitution. 1773 was the Boston Tea Party.

questions.question: In which century did the pandemic known as the Black Death ravage Europe, killing up to 60% of its population?
questions.explanation_correct: The Black Death peak occurred between 1347 and 1351, which lies in the 14th century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other centuries do not align with this pandemic.

questions.question: Which Spartan king led the Greek forces at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
questions.explanation_correct: Leonidas I died alongside his 300 Spartans defending the pass of Thermopylae against the Persians.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lycurgus was a legendary lawgiver. Agesilaus and Cleomenes were other historical Spartan kings.

questions.question: In which year did the Vietnam War end with the fall of Saigon?
questions.explanation_correct: Saigon fell to North Vietnamese forces on April 30, 1975, ending the war and reuniting the country.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1973 was when US combat troops withdrew. 1968 was the Tet Offensive. 1979 was the Sino-Vietnamese War.

questions.question: Which Macedonian king built one of the largest empires of the ancient world before dying in Babylon in 323 BC?
questions.explanation_correct: Alexander III of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire and expanded Greek influence into Asia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Philip II was his father. Perdiccas was a regent after his death. Ptolemy was his general who took Egypt.

questions.question: Which Viking explorer is widely believed to have reached North America (Vinland) around 1000 AD, long before Columbus?
questions.explanation_correct: Leif Erikson established a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in present-day Newfoundland around 1000 AD.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Erik the Red was his father (who settled Greenland). Ragnar is a legendary king. Harald Hardrada died in 1066.

questions.question: On which date (known as D-Day) did Allied forces land on the beaches of Normandy to liberate Western Europe?
questions.explanation_correct: Operation Overlord commenced on June 6, 1944, with massive amphibious and airborne landings.
questions.explanation_incorrect: May 8, 1945 was VE Day. September 3, 1939 was when Britain declared war on Germany.

questions.question: Which french military leader staged a coup d'état in 1799 and crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804?
questions.explanation_correct: Napoleon took power in the Coup of 18 Brumaire (1799) and was crowned Emperor in 1804.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Louis XIV was the Sun King. Robespierre led the Reign of Terror. Lafayette was a general in two revolutions.

questions.question: Which peace treaty, signed on June 28, 1919, officially ended the state of war between Germany and the Allied Powers?
questions.explanation_correct: The Treaty of Versailles was signed exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brest-Litovsk ended Russia's WWI role (1918). Treaty of Utrecht ended the Spanish Succession (1713). Treaty of Ghent ended the War of 1812.

questions.question: Who was the first official Emperor of the Roman Empire, ruling from 27 BC until 14 AD?
questions.explanation_correct: Born Octavian, Augustus became the sole ruler after defeating Antony and Cleopatra and established the Principate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Julius Caesar was a dictator. Tiberius was Augustus's successor. Nero ruled later.

questions.question: Which astronomer was placed under house arrest by the Inquisition in 1633 for championing heliocentrism?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo was tried by the Roman Inquisition for defending Copernicus's heliocentric view.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Copernicus died shortly after publishing. Kepler lived in protestant lands. Bruno was burned at the stake in 1600.

questions.question: Who was released from prison in 1990 after 27 years and became South Africa's first black president in 1994?
questions.explanation_correct: Mandela was a leader of the ANC who fought apartheid and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tutu was an archbishop. De Klerk was the white president who released Mandela. Biko died in prison in 1977.

questions.question: In which year did the United Kingdom vote to leave the European Union in a referendum (Brexit)?
questions.explanation_correct: The Brexit referendum took place on June 23, 2016, with 51.9% voting to leave the EU.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 2020 was the year the UK formally left. 2019 saw intense political gridlock. 2015 was the election preceding it.

questions.question: Which archaeological site in Peru, built by the Incas in the 15th century, is known as the 'Lost City of the Incas'?
questions.explanation_correct: Machu Picchu is situated on a mountain ridge above the Sacred Valley and was brought to world attention in 1911.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chichen Itza is Mayan (Mexico). Tikal is Mayan (Guatemala). Petra is Nabataean (Jordan).

questions.question: In which year did the Ottoman Empire capture Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire?
questions.explanation_correct: Sultan Mehmed II besieged and captured Constantinople in May 1453, ending over 1,000 years of Byzantine rule.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1492 was the Fall of Granada. 1204 was the Sack of Constantinople in the 4th Crusade. 1389 was the Battle of Kosovo.

questions.question: Who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled it until his death in 1976?
questions.explanation_correct: Mao Zedong proclaimed the PRC on October 1, 1949, after defeating the Nationalists in the Civil War.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Deng Xiaoping led market reforms later. Sun Yat-sen was the father of the 1911 republic. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan.

questions.question: In which year did World War II officially end with the formal surrender of Japan?
questions.explanation_correct: Japan signed the surrender documents on September 2, 1945, aboard the USS Missouri.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Germany surrendered in May 1945. The other options are prior years of the war.

questions.question: Who was the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom during most of World War II, from 1940 to 1945?
questions.explanation_correct: Winston Churchill took office in May 1940 and led Britain through its war effort.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chamberlain was PM before 1940. Attlee became PM in July 1945. Eden was PM in the 1950s.

questions.question: In which year did Martin Luther pin his Ninety-five Theses to the Wittenberg church door, starting the Protestant Reformation?
questions.explanation_correct: Luther posted his theses criticizing the sale of indulgences on October 31, 1517.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1521 was the Diet of Worms. 1534 was the English Act of Supremacy.

questions.question: Whose expedition completed the first circumnavigation of the globe between 1519 and 1522?
questions.explanation_correct: Magellan led the fleet, though he was killed in the Philippines; Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Da Gama sailed to India. Drake circumnavigated later (1577-1580). Polo traveled overland to China in the 13th century.

questions.question: Which empire was ruled by Cyrus the Great, Darius the Great, and Xerxes I?
questions.explanation_correct: The Achaemenid Persian Empire was founded by Cyrus in the 6th century BC and conquered by Alexander the Great.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other empires had different rulers (Rome, Assyria, Babylon).

questions.question: Which French queen was executed by guillotine in 1793 during the Reign of Terror?
questions.explanation_correct: Marie Antoinette, wife of Louis XVI, was convicted of high treason and executed on October 16, 1793.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Catherine and Marie de' Medici lived in earlier centuries. Josephine was Napoleon's first wife.

questions.question: In which year did the Soviet Union launch Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, initiating the Space Race?
questions.explanation_correct: Sputnik 1 was launched on October 4, 1957.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1961 was Gagarin's flight. 1969 was the Moon landing.

questions.question: Who patented the modern steam engine in 1769, dramatically accelerating the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation_correct: James Watt improved on Newcomen's engine design by adding a separate condenser, greatly improving fuel efficiency.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Newcomen built the first atmospheric engine. Stephenson built locomotives. Fulton built steamboats.

questions.question: In which year was the Berlin Wall built, physically dividing the city until its fall?
questions.explanation_correct: Construction of the Berlin Wall by East Germany began on August 13, 1961.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1945 was WWII end. 1949 was division of Germany into two states. 1968 was Prague Spring.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explanation_correct: Canberra was selected as the capital in 1908 as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sydney and Melbourne are the largest cities. Brisbane is the capital of Queensland.

questions.question: Which river is traditionally considered the longest in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: Geographers traditionally define the Nile (approx. 6,650 km) as the longest river, although recent studies suggest the Amazon might be longer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Amazon has the largest water volume. Yangtze is the longest in Asia. Mississippi is the main river in North America.

questions.question: What is the tallest mountain in Africa?
questions.explanation_correct: Mount Kilimanjaro is a volcanic mountain in Tanzania rising to 5,895 meters (19,341 ft) above sea level.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mount Kenya is the second-tallest. Ruwenzori is a mountain range. Mount Sinai is in Egypt (Asia).

questions.question: Which body of water is the largest enclosed inland body of water on Earth by area?
questions.explanation_correct: The Caspian Sea is classified as both a lake and a sea, with a surface area of 371,000 square kilometers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area. Dead Sea is a hypersaline lake. Baikal is the deepest lake.

questions.question: Which ocean is the largest and deepest on Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pacific Ocean covers about one-third of the Earth's surface and contains the Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Atlantic is the second largest, Indian is third, and Arctic is the smallest and shallowest.

questions.question: What is the largest island in the world (excluding continents)?
questions.explanation_correct: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark with an area of about 2.16 million square kilometers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: New Guinea is the second largest island, Borneo is third, and Madagascar is fourth.

questions.question: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: The Sahara Desert in North Africa covers about 9 million square kilometers, almost equal to the area of the US.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gobi is a cold desert in Asia. Kalahari is in southern Africa. Atacama is the driest non-polar desert.

questions.question: Which lake is the deepest in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Baikal in southern Siberia, Russia, has a maximum depth of 1,642 meters (5,387 ft) and holds 20% of Earth's fresh water.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tanganyika is the second deepest. Superior is largest by area. Victoria is the largest in Africa.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation_correct: Ottawa was selected as the capital by Queen Victoria in 1857 because of its central location between English and French speaking populations.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Toronto and Montreal are the largest cities. Vancouver is the largest on the Pacific coast.

questions.question: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
questions.explanation_correct: The Bering Strait connects the Bering Sea to the Chukchi Sea and is about 85 km (53 miles) wide at its narrowest point.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gibraltar connects the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. Malacca is in Southeast Asia. Bosporus divides Istanbul.

questions.question: Which of the following European countries is landlocked (completely surrounded by land)?
questions.explanation_correct: Switzerland is located in the Alps and borders France, Italy, Austria, Germany, and Liechtenstein, with no direct ocean access.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Germany, Poland, and Belgium all have coastlines on the Baltic Sea or North Sea.

questions.question: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.explanation_correct: Brasília is a planned city inaugurated in 1960 to serve as the new capital, moving it from the coast to the interior.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rio de Janeiro was the capital until 1960. São Paulo is the largest city. Salvador was the first capital.

questions.question: Which is the largest country by area in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation_correct: England covers about 130,279 square kilometers, which is over 50% of the total area of the UK.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scotland is second largest (approx. 77,900 sq km), Wales is third, and Northern Ireland is the smallest.

questions.question: Which river is the longest in Europe?
questions.explanation_correct: The Volga River flows entirely through Russia for 3,530 km (2,193 miles) before emptying into the Caspian Sea.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Danube is the second-longest (2,850 km). Rhine is a major river in Germany. Seine flows through Paris.

questions.question: Which mountain range is the longest continental mountain range in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: The Andes stretch over 7,000 km (4,350 miles) along the western coast of South America.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Himalayas are the highest. The Rockies are in North America. The Alps are in Europe.

questions.question: Which US state is the largest by area?
questions.explanation_correct: Alaska has an area of over 1.7 million square kilometers, more than double the size of Texas.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Texas is the second-largest, California third, and Montana fourth.

questions.question: Which country has the most natural lakes in the world, with over 3 million lakes?
questions.explanation_correct: Canada contains 9% of the world's renewable water supply and has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Finland is known as the 'Land of a Thousand Lakes' (about 187,000), but Canada has far more by total count.

questions.question: Which active volcano is the highest in Europe?
questions.explanation_correct: Mount Etna on the east coast of Sicily, Italy, is about 3,357 meters (11,014 ft) high.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vesuvius is near Naples. Stromboli is an island volcano. Mauna Loa is in Hawaii.

questions.question: Through which of these European countries does the Prime Meridian (0° longitude) pass?
questions.explanation_correct: The Prime Meridian passes through the UK, France, and Spain in Europe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Portugal lies west of the meridian. Italy and Germany lie to the east.

questions.question: Which canal, opened in 1914, connects the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean?
questions.explanation_correct: The Panama Canal cuts across the Isthmus of Panama, dramatically shortening shipping routes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean and Red seas. Kiel is in Germany. Erie is in New York.

questions.question: Which US city is known as the 'Windy City'?
questions.explanation_correct: Chicago was dubbed the 'Windy City' in the late 19th century, likely referring to its chilly lake breezes or its long-winded politicians.
questions.explanation_incorrect: New York is the Big Apple, Boston is Beantown, and Seattle is the Emerald City.

questions.question: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.explanation_correct: Wellington is the southernmost capital city of a sovereign state in the world, serving since 1865.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand. Christchurch is the largest in the South Island.

questions.question: Which of the following is the largest lake in Africa by surface area?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Victoria is the world's largest tropical lake, covering about 59,947 square kilometers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tanganyika is the longest and second deepest. Malawi is third largest. Chad is very shallow and shrinking.

questions.question: In which country can you find the ancient rock-cut city of Petra?
questions.explanation_correct: Petra, famous for its rock-cut architecture and water conduit system, is located in southern Jordan.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Egypt has Giza, Turkey has Ephesus, and Greece has the Acropolis.

questions.question: Which major river flows through London, England?
questions.explanation_correct: The River Thames flows through southern England and London, emptying into the North Sea.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Seine is in Paris. Danube flows through Central/Eastern Europe. Tiber flows through Rome.

questions.question: Which country is home to the world's highest plateau, often called the 'Roof of the World'?
questions.explanation_correct: The Tibetan Plateau covers about 2.5 million square kilometers and has an average elevation exceeding 4,500 meters.
questions.explanation_incorrect: India and Nepal border the plateau. Mongolia has its own lower steppes.

questions.question: Which country is the smallest island nation in the world by area, covering only 21 square kilometers?
questions.explanation_correct: Nauru is the smallest independent republic and smallest island nation in the world.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vatican City and Monaco are smaller but are city-states in Europe, not island nations.

questions.question: Which is the saltiest open sea on Earth (excluding hypersaline lakes like the Dead Sea)?
questions.explanation_correct: The Red Sea has high salinity (approx. 40‰) due to high evaporation, low rainfall, and lack of river inflows.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Baltic Sea is brackish. Mediterranean is moderately salty. Caribbean is normal oceanic salinity.

questions.question: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.explanation_correct: Tokyo was originally a fishing village called Edo; it became the capital in 1868 when Emperor Meiji moved his seat from Kyoto.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kyoto was the ancient capital. Osaka and Yokohama are other major Japanese cities.

questions.question: Which city-state is located at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula?
questions.explanation_correct: Singapore is a global financial hub consisting of one main island and 63 co-islands off the southern tip of Malaysia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hong Kong and Macau are Special Administrative Regions of China. Brunei is on Borneo island.

questions.question: Which country is shaped like a boot and extends into the Mediterranean Sea?
questions.explanation_correct: The Italian Peninsula has a distinctive boot shape (the 'lo Stivale') with Sicily at its toe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Greece has a jagged coastline of peninsulas. Spain and Portugal make up the blocky Iberian Peninsula.

questions.question: Which US state consists entirely of islands in the Pacific Ocean?
questions.explanation_correct: Hawaii is the only US state located outside North America, made up of an archipelago of 137 volcanic islands.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alaska is sub-arctic. California and Florida are on the mainland.

questions.question: What is the largest country by land area located entirely in Asia?
questions.explanation_correct: China is the largest country in Asia by area (excluding Russia, which is transcontinental and has its political center in Europe).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Russia is transcontinental. India is smaller than China. Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country.

questions.question: In which US city is the famous Golden Gate Bridge located?
questions.explanation_correct: The Golden Gate Bridge spans the Golden Gate strait, connecting San Francisco to Marin County.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Los Angeles has the Vincent Thomas Bridge. New York has the Brooklyn Bridge.

questions.question: Which country is the longest north-to-south country in the world, stretching over 4,270 km along the Andes?
questions.explanation_correct: Chile is an extremely narrow ribbon of land between the Andes and the Pacific.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Argentina is wide. Brazil is the largest country in South America. Peru is blocky.

questions.question: Which river has the largest volume of water discharge in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: The Amazon River accounts for about 20% of the world's total river flow, discharging more water than the next seven rivers combined.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nile is the longest. Congo is the deepest. Mississippi is the largest in North America.

questions.question: What is the capital of India?
questions.explanation_correct: New Delhi is an urban district within the metropolis of Delhi, serving as the seat of government since 1911.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mumbai is the financial center. Kolkata was the capital under British rule until 1911. Bangalore is the tech hub.

questions.question: Which mountain range forms the border between Spain and France?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pyrenees run for about 430 km (267 miles), dividing the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of Europe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alps are in Central Europe. Apennines run down Italy. Urals are in Russia.

questions.question: What is the capital of Iceland?
questions.explanation_correct: Reykjavík is the largest city in Iceland and the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are smaller towns in Iceland.

questions.question: Which country is the most populous in Africa?
questions.explanation_correct: Nigeria has a population exceeding 220 million people, making it the most populous country in Africa and 6th in the world.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ethiopia is second (approx. 120 million). Egypt is third (approx. 110 million).

questions.question: Which sea is located between Greece and Turkey?
questions.explanation_correct: The Aegean Sea is an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, containing thousands of Greek islands.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adriatic is between Italy and the Balkans. Ionian is west of Greece. Black Sea is north of Turkey.

questions.question: What is the largest lake entirely within the borders of Canada?
questions.explanation_correct: Great Bear Lake is the largest lake entirely in Canada (Lake Superior is shared with the US).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Great Slave is the deepest in North America. Winnipeg is smaller. Superior is shared.

questions.question: Which active volcanic island group in the Pacific belongs to the United States and has its capital at Honolulu?
questions.explanation_correct: The Hawaiian Islands are the 50th state of the USA, with Honolulu located on the island of Oahu.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Guam is an unincorporated territory. Samoa is split between US territory and an independent nation. Fiji is independent.

questions.question: What is the capital of Spain?
questions.explanation_correct: Madrid is the largest city in Spain and has been the capital since 1561 under Philip II.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia. Seville and Valencia are other major cities.

questions.question: Which South American country is home to the ancient ruins of Machu Picchu?
questions.explanation_correct: Machu Picchu is located in the Cusco Region of Peru, high in the Andes mountains.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ecuador, Bolivia, and Colombia also contain Andean peaks but not this Incan citadel.

questions.question: What is the capital of Egypt?
questions.explanation_correct: Cairo is the largest metropolitan area in Egypt and the Middle East, serving as capital since 969 AD.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alexandria is a major port. Giza is home to the pyramids. Luxor is a historical site.

questions.question: Which capital city has the River Danube flowing directly through its center?
questions.explanation_correct: The Danube divides the city of Budapest into its two historical halves: Buda and Pest.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Prague is on the Vltava. Warsaw is on the Vistula. Sofia is not on the Danube.

questions.question: Which country is the southernmost country on the North American continent?
questions.explanation_correct: Panama occupies the Isthmus of Panama, which links North America to South America.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Colombia is in South America. Costa Rica is north of Panama. Mexico is in northern Central America.

questions.question: What is the capital of South Korea?
questions.explanation_correct: Seoul is the capital and largest metropolis of South Korea, home to roughly half of the country's population.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Busan is the largest port city. Incheon is the main airport hub.

questions.question: Which country has the largest forest cover in Europe (excluding Russia)?
questions.explanation_correct: Finland is the most heavily forested country in Europe, with forests covering over 74% of its land area.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sweden has the second highest percentage. France and Germany have large forests but lower percentages of cover.

questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation_correct: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, completing one orbit in just 88 Earth days.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus is the second planet, Mars the fourth, and Jupiter the fifth.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation_correct: The skin is the largest organ, covering an area of about 1.5 - 2 square meters and making up about 15% of body weight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The liver is the largest internal organ. The brain weighs about 1.3-1.4 kg. The small intestine is long but has less mass.

questions.question: Who formulated the famous equation E = mc²?
questions.explanation_correct: Albert Einstein formulated this equation in 1905, representing the equivalence of mass and energy as part of his special theory of relativity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Newton discovered the laws of motion. Bohr created the atomic model. Hawking studied black holes.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for Gold?
questions.explanation_correct: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word for gold, 'aurum', meaning 'shining dawn'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ag is Silver (argentum), Fe is Iron (ferrum), and Cu is Copper (cuprum).

questions.question: Which particle in an atom has a negative electrical charge?
questions.explanation_correct: Electrons orbit the nucleus of an atom and carry a negative charge (-1e).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Protons are positive. Neutrons are neutral. Positrons are antimatter counterparts with a positive charge.

questions.question: How long (approximately) does it take for light from the Sun to reach Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the 150 million km distance to Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Light travels at 300,000 km/s. Other options do not match this speed and distance.

questions.question: Which gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation_correct: Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) and water to produce glucose, releasing oxygen (O2) as a byproduct.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oxygen is released. Nitrogen and hydrogen are not absorbed directly in gaseous form for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Who discovered the law of universal gravitation, published in 1687?
questions.explanation_correct: Sir Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation in his work 'Principia'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo studied gravity. Kepler described planetary motion. Descartes worked on philosophy and geometry.

questions.question: What is the most abundant element in the universe?
questions.explanation_correct: Hydrogen accounts for about 75% of the baryonic mass of the universe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Helium is the second most abundant (24%). Oxygen and carbon are much heavier and less common.

questions.question: How many pairs of chromosomes do humans typically have in each cell?
questions.explanation_correct: Humans have 46 chromosomes in total, organized into 23 pairs (one set from each parent).
questions.explanation_incorrect: 46 is the total number of chromosomes. Other numbers are incorrect for typical humans.

questions.question: Who is credited with discovering penicillin in 1928?
questions.explanation_correct: Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold called Penicillium notatum killed bacteria in his laboratory.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pasteur created the rabies vaccine. Koch identified tuberculosis bacteria. Jenner created the smallpox vaccine.

questions.question: What is the pH value of pure water at 25°C?
questions.explanation_correct: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of exactly 7.0.
questions.explanation_incorrect: pH 1 is strongly acidic. pH 14 is strongly basic. pH 5.5 is slightly acidic.

questions.question: What is the hardest natural mineral on Earth, scoring 10 on the Mohs scale?
questions.explanation_correct: Diamond's rigid carbon crystal structure makes it the hardest mineral, scratchable only by other diamonds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Corundum is 9. Topaz is 8. Quartz is 7.

questions.question: Which planet is known as the 'Red Planet' due to iron oxide on its surface?
questions.explanation_correct: Mars is covered in iron oxide (rust) dust, giving it a reddish appearance in the sky.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus is bright white/yellow. Mercury is grey. Jupiter is orange/brown striped.

questions.question: Which cell organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.explanation_correct: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's supply of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), used as a source of chemical energy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Chloroplasts do photosynthesis in plants. Nucleus holds DNA. Ribosomes make proteins.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula for common table salt?
questions.explanation_correct: Table salt is sodium chloride, composed of sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl) ions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: H2O is water. CO2 is carbon dioxide. NaHCO3 is baking soda.

questions.question: Which type of blood cells is primarily responsible for transporting oxygen?
questions.explanation_correct: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain hemoglobin, a protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it elsewhere.
questions.explanation_incorrect: White blood cells fight infection. Platelets cause clotting. Plasma is the liquid component.

questions.question: What is the square root of 144?
questions.explanation_correct: 12 multiplied by 12 equals exactly 144.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 11 squared is 121. 14 squared is 196. 16 squared is 256.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation_correct: The Ohm (symbol Ω) is the unit of electrical resistance, named after German physicist Georg Ohm.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Volt measures voltage. Ampere measures current. Watt measures power.

questions.question: Which organ in the human body produces insulin?
questions.explanation_correct: The pancreas contains islets of Langerhans which secrete insulin directly into the bloodstream to regulate glucose levels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The liver produces bile. Kidneys filter blood. The gallbladder stores bile.

questions.question: What was the name of the supercontinent that existed about 300 million ago?
questions.explanation_correct: Pangea was a single massive continent surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean before it broke up.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gondwana and Laurasia formed after Pangea split. Rodinia was an older supercontinent.

questions.question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum (approximately)?
questions.explanation_correct: Light travels at exactly 299,792,458 m/s, which is commonly rounded to 300,000 km/s.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 340 m/s is the speed of sound in air. Other options are incorrect.

questions.question: Which gas makes up approximately 78% of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation_correct: Nitrogen (N2) is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere, followed by oxygen at 21%.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oxygen is 21%. Argon is 0.9%. Carbon dioxide is about 0.04%.

questions.question: What is the term for a cell division process that results in four daughter cells each with half the chromosomes of the parent?
questions.explanation_correct: Meiosis is the specialized cell division that produces gametes (sperm and egg cells).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mitosis results in two identical somatic cells. Fission and budding are asexual reproduction methods.

questions.question: Which vitamin is synthesized in the human skin when exposed to UVB sunlight?
questions.explanation_correct: Sunlight triggers the conversion of cholesterol derivatives in skin cells to Vitamin D3.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vitamin C, A, and B12 must be obtained through food or supplements.

questions.question: Which celestial body was reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet in 2006?
questions.explanation_correct: The IAU redefined 'planet', excluding Pluto because it has not 'cleared its neighboring region' of other objects.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ceres was always an asteroid. Eris is another dwarf planet. Charon is Pluto's moon.

questions.question: Who formulated the three laws of classical motion?
questions.explanation_correct: Newton's laws of motion, describing inertia, force, and action-reaction, were published in 1687.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo studied gravity. Einstein worked on relativity. Maxwell formulated electromagnetic theory.

questions.question: What is the longest side of a right-angled triangle called?
questions.explanation_correct: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the 90-degree angle and is always the longest side.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adjacent and opposite sides meet at the right angle. Median connects a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

questions.question: What is the collective name for elements in Group 18 of the periodic table, known for low reactivity?
questions.explanation_correct: Noble gases (helium, neon, argon, etc.) have full valence electron shells, making them highly stable.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Halogens are highly reactive non-metals. Alkali metals are highly reactive metals. Lanthanides are rare earth elements.

questions.question: What are proteins made of?
questions.explanation_correct: Proteins are polymers constructed from chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fatty acids build lipids. Nucleotides build nucleic acids (DNA/RNA). Monosaccharides build carbohydrates.

questions.question: How many bits are in a standard byte?
questions.explanation_correct: A byte is a unit of digital information consisting of 8 bits, representing up to 256 values.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 4 bits is a nibble. 16 bits is a word in older 16-bit systems.

questions.question: Who proposed the heliocentric theory of the solar system in 1543?
questions.explanation_correct: Nicolaus Copernicus published 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium', putting the Sun at the center of the solar system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kepler proved elliptical orbits. Galileo observed moons of Jupiter. Brahe made astronomical observations.

questions.question: What is the unit of wave frequency in the SI system?
questions.explanation_correct: One Hertz is defined as one cycle per second (1/s).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Decibel measures sound intensity. Meters per second measures speed. Joule measures energy.

questions.question: Which acid is typically found in lead-acid car batteries?
questions.explanation_correct: Lead-acid batteries use a solution of sulfuric acid (H2SO4) as the electrolyte.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hydrochloric (HCl) and nitric (HNO3) acids are too corrosive. Acetic acid is vinegar.

questions.question: Which of the following is the fastest land animal?
questions.explanation_correct: The cheetah can reach speeds of 100-120 km/h (60-75 mph) in short bursts.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pronghorn is the second fastest. Lions reach 80 km/h. Ostrich is the fastest bird (70 km/h).

questions.question: What is the name of our home galaxy?
questions.explanation_correct: The Solar System is located within the Orion Arm of the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Andromeda is the closest spiral galaxy. Triangulum is another local group galaxy. Magellanic Clouds are dwarf satellite galaxies.

questions.question: What is the temperature of absolute zero in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation_correct: Absolute zero (0 Kelvin) is the theoretical limit where all molecular motion stops, corresponding to -273.15°C.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 0°C is water freezing. -459.67°F is absolute zero in Fahrenheit, not Celsius.

questions.question: Which element is the primary component of coal, diamond, and graphite?
questions.explanation_correct: Diamonds and graphite are allotropes of pure carbon (C). Coal is also mostly carbon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Silicon, sulfur, and hydrogen are different elements.

questions.question: What is the largest living mammal on Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: The blue whale can reach lengths of over 30 meters and weigh up to 190 tonnes, making it the largest animal known to have existed.
questions.explanation_incorrect: African Elephant is the largest land mammal. Sperm Whale is the largest toothed predator. Whale Shark is a fish, not a mammal.

questions.question: What is the sum of the interior angles of a triangle in Euclidean geometry?
questions.explanation_correct: In Euclidean geometry, the sum of angles of any triangle is always 180 degrees.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 360 degrees is the sum for quadrilaterals. Others are incorrect.

questions.question: Which scientist formulated the Uncertainty Principle, a foundation of quantum mechanics?
questions.explanation_correct: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927) states that one cannot measure both position and momentum of a particle with absolute precision.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Schrödinger made the wave equation. Planck proposed quantum constant. Einstein opposed quantum uncertainty.

questions.question: Which gas is dissolved in carbonated beverages to create bubbles?
questions.explanation_correct: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is dissolved under pressure in water, forming carbonic acid and escaping as bubbles when opened.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other gases are not used for carbonation.

questions.question: What is the term for a bacterial reproduction method where a cell splits into two identical clones?
questions.explanation_correct: Bacteria replicate through binary fission, duplicating their DNA and dividing into two.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Conjugation is horizontal gene transfer. Budding is typical of yeasts. Mitosis is eukaryotic cell division.

questions.question: Which scale is used to measure wind speed based on observed sea or land conditions?
questions.explanation_correct: The Beaufort scale ranges from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force), created by Francis Beaufort in 1805.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Richter measures earthquakes. Celsius measures temperature. Fujita measures tornado damage.

questions.question: Which system in the human body is responsible for defending against pathogens like bacteria and viruses?
questions.explanation_correct: The immune system identifies and fights foreign invaders using white blood cells and antibodies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lymphatic system supports immune transport. Nervous and digestive systems serve other vital functions.

questions.question: What is the closest star system to the Sun, about 4.24 light-years away?
questions.explanation_correct: Alpha Centauri is a triple star system, with Proxima Centauri being the closest individual star.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sirius is 8.6 ly away. Polaris is over 300 ly away. Betelgeuse is a distant red supergiant.

questions.question: Which scientist formulated the wave equation used in quantum mechanics to describe wave-particle duality?
questions.explanation_correct: Schrödinger published his wave equation in 1926, laying the groundwork for wave mechanics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Heisenberg used matrix mechanics. Bohr made the atomic orbit model. De Broglie proposed wave-particle duality.

questions.question: What is the common name for the compound sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3)?
questions.explanation_correct: Sodium bicarbonate is a white crystalline solid used in baking as a leavening agent, known as baking soda.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Table salt is NaCl. Bleach is sodium hypochlorite. Vinegar is acetic acid.

questions.question: Which of the following mammals is the only one capable of sustained, active flight?
questions.explanation_correct: Bats have webbed wings stretched over their elongated fingers, enabling true flight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lemurs and squirrels only glide. Penguins are flightless birds.

questions.question: What term describes the role and position a species has in its environment, including its resource use?
questions.explanation_correct: An ecological niche encompasses how a species survives, behaves, and interacts within its habitat.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Habitat is the physical place. Biome is a large geographical area. Ecosystem includes biotic and abiotic factors.

questions.question: Who painted the famous artwork 'Mona Lisa'?
questions.explanation_correct: The Mona Lisa (La Gioconda) was painted by the Italian Renaissance polymath Leonardo da Vinci in the early 16th century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Michelangelo sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel. Raphael painted Madonnas. Van Gogh painted Starry Night.

questions.question: Who wrote the play 'Romeo and Juliet'?
questions.explanation_correct: Romeo and Juliet is an early tragedy written by William Shakespeare around 1595-1597.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Marlowe was a contemporary dramatist. Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales. Milton wrote Paradise Lost.

questions.question: Who was the Greek god of the sea and earthquakes?
questions.explanation_correct: Poseidon, brother of Zeus and Hades, was the ruler of the seas, ocean storms, and earthquakes, depicted holding a trident.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zeus was god of sky and lightning. Hades ruled the Underworld. Ares was god of war.

questions.question: Which Norwegian artist painted the iconic expressionist work 'The Scream'?
questions.explanation_correct: Edvard Munch created four versions of 'The Scream' between 1893 and 1910.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Van Gogh, Picasso, and Monet were other legendary painters of different styles (Post-Impressionism, Cubism, Impressionism).

questions.question: Which composer, despite going deaf, composed the famous Ninth Symphony containing the 'Ode to Joy'?
questions.explanation_correct: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony in 1824 when he was almost completely deaf.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mozart died young composing Requiem. Bach was a Baroque master. Chopin composed mainly for solo piano.

questions.question: Who was the twin brother of Remus and the legendary founder of Rome in 753 BC?
questions.explanation_correct: According to Roman legend, Romulus and Remus were raised by a she-wolf; Romulus later killed Remus and founded Rome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aeneas was a Trojan ancestor. Numa was the second king of Rome.

questions.question: Which Spanish artist is widely regarded as the co-founder of the Cubist movement?
questions.explanation_correct: Picasso, along with Georges Braque, pioneered Cubism in the early 20th century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dalí was a Surrealist. Goya and Velázquez were older Spanish masters.

questions.question: Who wrote the classic 19th-century French novel 'Les Misérables'?
questions.explanation_correct: Victor Hugo published 'Les Misérables' in 1862, depicting social injustice in France.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Flaubert wrote Madame Bovary. Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers. Zola wrote Germinal.

questions.question: Which Renaissance master sculpted the marble statue of David in Florence?
questions.explanation_correct: Michelangelo Buonarroti sculpted the five-meter statue of David between 1501 and 1504.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Donatello sculpted an earlier bronze David. Bernini sculpted a baroque David in action. Leonardo was not the sculptor.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek playwright wrote the tragedy 'Oedipus Rex'?
questions.explanation_correct: Sophocles wrote 'Oedipus Rex' around 429 BC, detailing Oedipus's tragic fate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Aeschylus and Euripides were other tragedy writers. Aristophanes wrote comedies.

questions.question: Which Dutch painter is famous for 'Girl with a Pearl Earring', often called the 'Mona Lisa of the North'?
questions.explanation_correct: Vermeer painted 'Girl with a Pearl Earring' around 1665.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rembrandt painted The Night Watch. Van Gogh painted Starry Night. Bosch painted The Garden of Earthly Delights.

questions.question: In which European country is the famous Leaning Tower of Pisa located?
questions.explanation_correct: The tower is the freestanding bell tower of the cathedral of Pisa, Italy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other countries have famous monuments, but the Leaning Tower is in Italy.

questions.question: What architectural style is characterized by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses (e.g., Notre-Dame de Paris)?
questions.explanation_correct: Gothic architecture flourished in Europe during the High and Late Middle Ages, emphasizing light and height.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Romanesque had thick walls and round arches. Renaissance featured classical geometry. Baroque used dramatic ornamentation.

questions.question: Which French painter is considered a founder of French Impressionism, with his painting 'Impression, Sunrise' giving the movement its name?
questions.explanation_correct: Claude Monet painted the work in 1872, exhibiting it in 1874, which led critics to coin the term 'Impressionism'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Manet, Renoir, and Degas were other major impressionist painters, but Monet's title named the movement.

questions.question: Who wrote the Russian literary classic 'Crime and Punishment', centering on Rodion Raskolnikov?
questions.explanation_correct: Dostoevsky published the psychological novel in 1866.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tolstoy wrote War and Peace. Chekhov wrote plays like The Cherry Orchard. Gogol wrote Dead Souls.

questions.question: Who was the Roman equivalent of the Greek god Zeus, ruling sky and thunder?
questions.explanation_correct: Jupiter (or Jove) was the king of the Roman pantheon, matching Zeus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Neptune is Poseidon. Pluto is Hades. Mars is Ares.

questions.question: Which famous ancient Greek marble sculpture, currently in the Louvre, represents the goddess of victory without arms and head?
questions.explanation_correct: The Winged Victory of Samothrace (Nike) was created in the 2nd century BC and stands at the grand staircase of the Louvre.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus de Milo is a statue of Aphrodite. Kore is an archaic female statue. Caryatids are columns carved as women.

questions.question: Who wrote the epic high-fantasy novel 'The Lord of the Rings'?
questions.explanation_correct: J.R.R. Tolkien wrote the work as a sequel to his 1937 novel The Hobbit.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lewis wrote Narnia. Martin wrote A Song of Ice and Fire. Rowling wrote Harry Potter.

questions.question: Which Dutch Post-Impressionist painter cut off his own ear and later painted an self-portrait with his head bandaged?
questions.explanation_correct: Van Gogh cut off his left ear during a mental breakdown in Arles in 1888.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gauguin was his friend who was present. Rembrandt lived in the 17th century. Mondrian was a 20th-century abstract painter.

questions.question: Which famous Roman temple features a giant concrete dome with a central opening (oculus)?
questions.explanation_correct: The Pantheon in Rome was rebuilt by Emperor Hadrian around 126 AD, featuring the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Colosseum is an amphitheater. Parthenon is in Athens, Greece.

questions.question: Who was the Greek god of fire, metalworking, and stone masonry, married to Aphrodite?
questions.explanation_correct: Hephaestus was the blacksmith god who forged weapons for the gods in his workshop under Mount Etna.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ares was the god of war. Hermes was the messenger. Apollo was the god of music and light.

questions.question: Who wrote the 14th-century Italian epic 'The Divine Comedy' describing a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven?
questions.explanation_correct: Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy between 1308 and 1321, shaping Italian literature.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Petrarch wrote Canzoniere. Boccaccio wrote Decameron. Virgil was Dante's guide in the poem.

questions.question: Which Spanish Surrealist painter is famous for his 1931 painting 'The Persistence of Memory', featuring melting clocks?
questions.explanation_correct: Salvador Dalí created 'The Persistence of Memory', embodying the dream-like qualities of Surrealism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Miró was another surrealist. Picasso founded Cubism. Goya was a Romantic painter.

questions.question: In which city is the famous palace complex of Versailles located?
questions.explanation_correct: The Palace of Versailles was built by King Louis XIV in the suburb of Versailles, 20 km southwest of Paris.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are different locations in France.

questions.question: Which Italian composer wrote the famous set of four violin concertos titled 'The Four Seasons'?
questions.explanation_correct: Vivaldi composed 'The Four Seasons' (Le quattro stagioni) around 1720, depicting seasonal scenes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monteverdi was an early opera pioneer. Verdi and Puccini were 19th and 20th-century opera composers.

questions.question: Who stole fire from the Greek gods on Mount Olympus and gave it to humanity, resulting in his eternal punishment?
questions.explanation_correct: Zeus punished Prometheus by chaining him to a rock where an eagle would eat his liver every day, only for it to grow back overnight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sisyphus rolled a boulder. Tantalus suffered in water. Hercules was a demigod hero.

questions.question: Who wrote the Spanish classic 'Don Quixote' about a delusional knight fighting windmills?
questions.explanation_correct: Cervantes published 'Don Quixote' in two parts (1605 and 1615), mocking traditional chivalric romances.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lope de Vega was a golden age playwright. Lorca was a 20th-century poet. Márquez was Colombian.

questions.question: In which Spanish city is the Sagrada Família church, designed by Antoni Gaudí, located?
questions.explanation_correct: The Sagrada Família has been under construction in Barcelona since 1882.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are different cities in Spain.

questions.question: What is the name of the three-headed dog that guards the entrance to the underworld in Greek mythology?
questions.explanation_correct: Cerberus prevented the dead from escaping the underworld and the living from entering.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Minotaur was half-bull. Harpy was a bird-woman. Chimera was a fire-breathing hybrid monster.

questions.question: Who wrote the Gothic horror novel 'Dracula', published in 1897?
questions.explanation_correct: Irish author Bram Stoker created the character of Count Dracula and established many vampire tropes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein. Poe wrote Gothic short stories. Lovecraft created cosmic horror.

questions.question: Which Austrian symbolist painter created the famous gold-leaf decorated painting 'The Kiss'?
questions.explanation_correct: Gustav Klimt painted 'The Kiss' during his 'Golden Phase' between 1907 and 1908.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Schiele and Kokoschka were expressionists. Mucha was a Czech Art Nouveau illustrator.

questions.question: Who wrote the modern play 'Waiting for Godot', a cornerstone of the Theatre of the Absurd?
questions.explanation_correct: French/Irish playwright Samuel Beckett wrote 'Waiting for Godot' in French ('En attendant Godot') in the late 1940s.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Miller wrote Death of a Salesman. Williams wrote A Streetcar Named Desire. O'Neill wrote Long Day's Journey into Night.

questions.question: Which Russian composer wrote the music for the classic ballets 'Swan Lake' and 'The Nutcracker'?
questions.explanation_correct: Tchaikovsky's late 19th-century scores are among the most famous ballet compositions in history.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Prokofiev composed Romeo and Juliet. Stravinsky composed The Rite of Spring. Shostakovich composed symphonies.

questions.question: In Norse mythology, what is the name of the home of the gods, connected to Midgard by the Bifröst bridge?
questions.explanation_correct: Asgard is one of the Nine Worlds, ruled by Odin and home to the Æsir gods.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Valhalla is Odin's hall within Asgard. Helheim is the underworld. Jötunheim is the land of giants.

questions.question: Which classic American novel by F. Scott Fitzgerald depicts the roaring twenties and the elusive Jay Gatsby?
questions.explanation_correct: The Great Gatsby was published in 1925, exploring themes of wealth, love, and the American Dream.
questions.explanation_incorrect: To Kill a Mockingbird is by Harper Lee. Grapes of Wrath is by John Steinbeck. Moby-Dick is by Herman Melville.

questions.question: Which French sculptor created 'The Thinker' (Le Penseur) as part of a larger commission titled 'The Gates of Hell'?
questions.explanation_correct: Auguste Rodin conceived the bronze sculpture around 1880, casting it as a standalone piece in 1904.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Degas is known for Little Dancer Aged Fourteen. Claudel was Rodin's collaborator. Bernini was a Baroque sculptor.

questions.question: Who was the Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, corresponding to the Greek Athena?
questions.explanation_correct: Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom, medicine, commerce, and the arts.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Diana was the goddess of the hunt (Artemis). Venus was the goddess of love (Afrodite). Juno was the queen (Hera).

questions.question: Which American artist is famous for pioneering Abstract Expressionism with his 'drip painting' technique?
questions.explanation_correct: Jackson Pollock was a leading force of the action painting movement, pouring household paint onto horizontal canvases.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Warhol and Lichtenstein were Pop artists. Rothko did Color Field painting.

questions.question: Who wrote the 1851 classic novel 'Moby-Dick' about Captain Ahab's obsessive hunt for a white whale?
questions.explanation_correct: Herman Melville's masterpiece initially flopped but was later recognized as a peak of American literature.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hawthorne wrote The Scarlet Letter. Twain wrote Huckleberry Finn. Poe wrote poetry and tales.

questions.question: Which Greek philosopher was the tutor of Alexander the Great and a student of Plato?
questions.explanation_correct: Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy and later founded the Lyceum, tutoring Alexander around 343 BC.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Socrates was Plato's teacher. Epicurus and Zeno founded Epicureanism and Stoicism later.

questions.question: What is the name of the iconic white marble mausoleum in India built by Shah Jahan?
questions.explanation_correct: The Taj Mahal in Agra was completed around 1648 as a monument of love for Mumtaz Mahal.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hawa Mahal is in Jaipur. Red Fort is in Delhi. Qutub Minar is a minaret in Delhi.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Odyssey' and 'The Iliad', the foundational works of ancient Greek literature?
questions.explanation_correct: Homer is the legendary blind poet to whom these two epic poems are attributed (c. 8th century BC).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Virgil wrote the Aeneid. Ovid wrote Metamorphoses. Hesiod was another early Greek poet.

questions.question: Which French artist painted 'Liberty Leading the People' commemorating the July Revolution of 1830?
questions.explanation_correct: Delacroix's painting depicts Liberty as a bare-breasted woman holding the tricolor flag.
questions.explanation_incorrect: David was a Neoclassicist (Death of Marat). Géricault painted The Raft of the Medusa. Ingres was a rival classicist.

questions.question: Which German philosopher wrote 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' and proclaimed that 'God is dead'?
questions.explanation_correct: Nietzsche critique of Christian morality and concept of the Übermensch were detailed in his works.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kant wrote Critique of Pure Reason. Marx wrote Das Kapital. Schopenhauer wrote World as Will and Representation.

questions.question: Which Italian director is famous for pioneering the Spaghetti Western genre with his 'Dollars Trilogy'?
questions.explanation_correct: Sergio Leone directed A Fistful of Dollars, For a Few Dollars More, and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fellini, Visconti, and Bertolucci were famous for art-house and dramatic films.

questions.question: Who was the Greek goddess of the hearth and home, one of the original Twelve Olympians?
questions.explanation_correct: Hestia was the oldest daughter of Cronus and Rhea, presiding over domestic life.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Demeter was the goddess of harvest. Persephone was queen of the underworld. Iris was the messenger rainbow goddess.

questions.question: Who wrote the classic children's book 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland' under the pen name Lewis Carroll?
questions.explanation_correct: Charles Dodgson was an Oxford mathematician who wrote under the pseudonym Lewis Carroll.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eric Blair was George Orwell. Samuel Clemens was Mark Twain. Mary Ann Evans was George Eliot.

questions.question: Which art movement, originating in Italy, is characterized by a rebirth of interest in classical antiquity (14th-17th centuries)?
questions.explanation_correct: The Renaissance (Rinascimento) saw a revival of classical learning, perspective in painting, and humanism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Baroque followed the Renaissance with more drama. Mannerism was a transitional style. Classicism is a broader aesthetic.

questions.question: Which iconic Sydney building, designed by Jørn Utzon, resembles sails or shells and opened in 1973?
questions.explanation_correct: The Sydney Opera House is a masterpiece of 20th-century expressionist architecture.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Harbour Bridge is a steel arch bridge. Sydney Tower is a metallic spire.

questions.question: Which ancient Egyptian queen's bust, discovered in 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt, is a symbol of feminine beauty?
questions.explanation_correct: The painted stucco-coated limestone bust of Nefertiti is housed in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler. Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh. Nefertari was Ramesses II's queen.

questions.question: How often are the Summer Olympic Games held under normal circumstances?
questions.explanation_correct: The Summer Olympic Games are held every 4 years, separated by two years from the Winter Games.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The 2-year interval separates winter and summer, but each occurs on a 4-year cycle.

questions.question: Which country has won the most FIFA World Cup titles (as of 2026)?
questions.explanation_correct: Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup a record five times (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Germany and Italy have four titles each. Argentina has three titles.

questions.question: On which playing surface is the Wimbledon tennis tournament played?
questions.explanation_correct: Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only Grand Slam still played on traditional grass courts.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Roland Garros is played on clay. US Open and Australian Open are played on hard courts.

questions.question: What is the official distance of a standard marathon race?
questions.explanation_correct: The marathon distance is 42 kilometers and 195 meters (26 miles 385 yards), standardized in 1921.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 21.097 km is a half marathon. Others are rounded metric distances.

questions.question: Which league is the premier professional men's basketball league in North America?
questions.explanation_correct: The NBA (National Basketball Association) was founded in 1946 and features 30 teams.
questions.explanation_incorrect: NFL is American football. NHL is ice hockey. MLB is baseball.

questions.question: Which prestigious multi-stage bicycle race is held annually, primarily in France, in July?
questions.explanation_correct: The Tour de France is the oldest and most famous of the three cycling Grand Tours.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Giro is in Italy. Vuelta is in Spain. Tour de Pologne is in Poland.

questions.question: Which driver holds the record for most Formula One World Championship titles, tied with Lewis Hamilton?
questions.explanation_correct: German driver Michael Schumacher won 7 world titles (two with Benetton, five with Ferrari).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Senna won 3. Vettel won 4. Prost won 4.

questions.question: Which legendary heavyweight boxer was born Cassius Clay and famously declared 'Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee'?
questions.explanation_correct: Muhammad Ali won the world heavyweight championship three times and is widely considered one of the greatest athletes of all time.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tyson, Frazier, and Foreman were other heavyweight champions.

questions.question: Who holds the men's 100 meters world record with a time of 9.58 seconds?
questions.explanation_correct: Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt set the record at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gay and Blake have personal bests of 9.69. Carl Lewis set records in the 1980s.

questions.question: How long is a standard professional football match (excluding extra time)?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard match consists of two halves of 45 minutes, plus stoppage time added by the referee.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rugby matches are 80 minutes. Ice hockey has three 20-minute periods (60 minutes total).

questions.question: Which trophy is awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff champion?
questions.explanation_correct: The Stanley Cup is the oldest trophy in North American professional sports, dating back to 1893.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lombardi is NFL. Larry O'Brien is NBA. Commissioner's is MLB.

questions.question: Which city hosted the 2024 Summer Olympic Games?
questions.explanation_correct: Paris hosted the Summer Olympics in July-August 2024, matching London as a three-time host.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tokyo hosted in 2021. Los Angeles will host in 2028.

questions.question: In which country did the modern game of golf originate in the 15th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Modern golf was developed in Scotland, where the first written record of the game was a ban in 1457.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other countries had stick-and-ball games, but the 18-hole format was defined in Scotland.

questions.question: Who is the most decorated Olympian of all time, with 28 medals, including 23 golds?
questions.explanation_correct: American swimmer Michael Phelps holds the records for most Olympic gold medals and total medals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Spitz won 9 golds. Thorpe won 5. Dressel has 7 golds but fewer overall.

questions.question: What is the championship game of the National Football League (NFL) called?
questions.explanation_correct: The Super Bowl is played annually in early February, matching the champions of the AFC and NFC.
questions.explanation_incorrect: World Series is baseball. Stanley Cup is hockey. MLS Cup is soccer.

questions.question: What shape is the ball used in rugby union and rugby league?
questions.explanation_correct: Rugby balls are oval, designed to be easily held under the arm and thrown backward.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other balls are round or spherical.

questions.question: Who has won the most men's singles Grand Slam titles in tennis history (as of 2026)?
questions.explanation_correct: Serbian Novak Djokovic holds the record with 24 Grand Slam singles titles.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nadal has 22. Federer has 20. Sampras retired with 14.

questions.question: In which track event did Usain Bolt win gold medals at three consecutive Olympics (2008, 2012, 2016)?
questions.explanation_correct: Bolt completed the 'triple-double', winning the 100m and 200m at Beijing, London, and Rio.
questions.explanation_incorrect: He did not compete in the 400m or long jump at the Olympics.

questions.question: How many players are on the field for the defending team in a baseball game?
questions.explanation_correct: The defending team has 9 players on the field: pitcher, catcher, four infielders, and three outfielders.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 11 is soccer. 7 is water polo. 5 is basketball.

questions.question: What are the two sets of three wooden stakes at each end of the pitch in cricket called?
questions.explanation_correct: The wicket consists of three stumps topped by two wooden bails.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Stumps are the vertical stakes. Bails are the horizontal pieces. Crease is the boundary line.

questions.question: In which sport is the X Games held annually?
questions.explanation_correct: The X Games features action sports like skateboarding, BMX, freestyle motocross, snowboarding, and skiing.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Surfing has separate tours. Bungee is not an X Games sport.

questions.question: Which annual 24-hour endurance race is held near the town of Le Mans, France?
questions.explanation_correct: The 24 Hours of Le Mans is the world's oldest active sports car race in endurance racing, held since 1923.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monaco GP is F1. Daytona 500 is NASCAR. Indy 500 is IndyCar.

questions.question: What color belt represents the highest rank attainable in traditional judo?
questions.explanation_correct: In judo, the 10th dan (highest rank) is awarded a red belt, representing the full circle of learning.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Black is the starting dan rank. White is for beginners. Gold is not a belt rank.

questions.question: Which club did Lionel Messi play for during most of his professional career, from 2004 to 2021?
questions.explanation_correct: Messi joined Barcelona's youth academy in 2000 and won 35 trophies with the first team.
questions.explanation_incorrect: He played for PSG (2021-2023) and Inter Miami later. Real Madrid is Barca's main rival.

questions.question: Which winter sport combines cross-country skiing and rifle shooting?
questions.explanation_correct: The biathlon requires athletes to ski a distance, then stop at shooting ranges to hit targets under high heart rate.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nordic Combined is ski jumping and cross-country. Skeleton and luge are sledding sports.

questions.question: Who is the NBA's all-time leading scorer, passing Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's record in 2023?
questions.explanation_correct: LeBron James broke the record on February 7, 2023, and became the first player to surpass 40,000 career points.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kareem held the record since 1984. Jordan is 5th. Bryant is 4th.

questions.question: What is the value of the black ball in snooker?
questions.explanation_correct: The black ball is the highest-value color ball in snooker, worth 7 points.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pink is 6. Blue is 5. Brown is 4.

questions.question: How many points does a player need to win a game of table tennis under modern rules?
questions.explanation_correct: ITTF changed the rules in 2001, reducing the game from 21 points to 11 (with a 2-point margin).
