questions.explanation_incorrect: 21 was the old rule. 15 and 10 are not used.

questions.question: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held in 1896?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1896 Summer Olympics were held in Athens, Greece, honoring the ancient birthplace.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Olympia hosted the ancient games. Paris hosted in 1900. Rome hosted in 1960.

questions.question: How many players from each team are on the field during an American football play?
questions.explanation_correct: Both offense and defense field exactly 11 players during a play in the NFL.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Canadian football fields 12. Rugby union fields 15.

questions.question: How many 20-minute periods are in a regulation ice hockey game?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard hockey game has three 20-minute periods, separated by 15-minute intermissions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Basketball has four quarters. Soccer has two halves.

questions.question: What is the name of the defensive specialist player in volleyball who wears a different colored jersey?
questions.explanation_correct: The libero position was introduced in 1998, restricted to back-row play and forbidden from serving or attacking.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Setters run the offense. Hitter and opposite are attacking positions.

questions.question: What is the title given to a horse that wins the Kentucky Derby, Preakness Stakes, and Belmont Stakes?
questions.explanation_correct: The Triple Crown of Thoroughbred Racing is one of the hardest accomplishments in sport, won by only 13 horses.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Grand Slam is tennis. Others are not official horse racing terms.

questions.question: In which athletics event does a competitor use a flexible pole to jump over a bar?
questions.explanation_correct: The pole vault requires speed and gymnastic ability to clear heights over 6 meters.
questions.explanation_incorrect: High jump is done without a pole. Long and triple jump are horizontal jumps.

questions.question: Which water sport has team positions called 'hole man' (center forward) and 'hole guard' (center defender)?
questions.explanation_correct: Water polo is a team sport played in a pool, where the center positions are crucial for offense and defense.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rowing and diving are individual or tandem sports.

questions.question: In which country is the historic town of Marathon, from which the long-distance race takes its name?
questions.explanation_correct: Marathon is a town in Greece, site of the 490 BC battle. Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens to deliver news of victory.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other Mediterranean countries are not home to this town.

questions.question: Who won four gold medals in artistic gymnastics at the 2016 Rio Olympics, representing the United States?
questions.explanation_correct: Simone Biles won individual gold in all-around, vault, and floor, plus team gold.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Douglas won in 2012. Raisman was her teammate. Comăneci competed in the 1970s.

questions.question: Which English football club has won the most UEFA Champions League titles (as of 2026)?
questions.explanation_correct: Liverpool FC has won the Champions League / European Cup six times.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Manchester United has won three times. Chelsea has won twice. Manchester City has won once.

questions.question: What is the projectile used in the game of badminton called?
questions.explanation_correct: A shuttlecock (often called a shuttle or birdie) consists of 16 feathers or synthetic nylon stuck into a cork base.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Puck is used in hockey. Ball is not the official name.

questions.question: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is played on red clay courts?
questions.explanation_correct: The French Open, held in Paris, is the only Grand Slam played on clay, known for slowing down the ball.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Wimbledon is grass. US and Australian Opens are played on acrylic hard courts.

questions.question: Which movie was the first in history to win a record 11 Academy Awards (Oscars)?
options: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003)
questions.explanation_correct: Ben-Hur (directed by William Wyler) won 11 Oscars in 1960. This record was later tied by Titanic and Return of the King.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titanic and Return of the King also won 11 but years later. Gone with the Wind won 8 Oscars.

questions.question: In which city is the popular sitcom 'Friends' set?
questions.explanation_correct: Friends is set in Greenwich Village, Manhattan, New York City, although it was filmed in studios in Burbank, California.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other US cities; none served as the home of the six main friends.

questions.question: Who is widely referred to as the 'King of Pop'?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Jackson was dubbed the 'King of Pop' due to his massive chart-topping success, albums like 'Thriller', and iconic dance moves.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Elvis Presley is the 'King of Rock and Roll'. Prince and Bowie are legendary artists but have different titles.

questions.question: Who directed the blockbuster movies 'Jaws', 'E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial', and 'Jurassic Park'?
questions.explanation_correct: Steven Spielberg is one of the co-founders of the DreamWorks studio and one of the most successful directors in Hollywood history.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lucas created Star Wars. Cameron directed Titanic. Scorsese is known for gangster films.

questions.question: Who is the high school chemistry teacher turned meth kingpin in the AMC series 'Breaking Bad'?
questions.explanation_correct: Walter White (played by Bryan Cranston) adopts the pseudonym 'Heisenberg' after being diagnosed with lung cancer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jesse was his partner. Saul was his lawyer. Hank was his DEA brother-in-law.

questions.question: Which English rock band, formed in Liverpool in 1960, is the best-selling music band in history?
questions.explanation_correct: The Beatles, consisting of Lennon, McCartney, Harrison, and Starr, revolutionized popular music.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, and Queen are also top-sellers but behind The Beatles.

questions.question: Which actor played the character Jack Dawson in the 1997 epic romance 'Titanic'?
questions.explanation_correct: Leonardo DiCaprio starred alongside Kate Winslet, launching him into international superstardom.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other actors were considered but did not get the role.

questions.question: Which TV network produced the hit fantasy drama series 'Game of Thrones'?
questions.explanation_correct: HBO broadcasted the series, based on George R.R. Martin's books, from 2011 to 2019.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Netflix, Showtime, and AMC have their own original series but did not produce Game of Thrones.

questions.question: Which Swedish pop group won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974 with the song 'Waterloo'?
questions.explanation_correct: ABBA's victory in Brighton propelled them to global charts, making them one of the most successful bands ever.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Roxette and Ace of Base are also Swedish but did not win Eurovision. Europe is known for The Final Countdown.

questions.question: Which 1999 sci-fi film stars Keanu Reeves as Neo, a hacker who discovers the world is a simulation?
questions.explanation_correct: The Matrix, directed by the Wachowskis, popularized the 'bullet time' effect and won four Oscars.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Blade Runner is from 1982. Inception is 2010. Interstellar is 2014.

questions.question: Who directed the film adaptation of 'The Lord of the Rings' trilogy?
questions.explanation_correct: New Zealand director Peter Jackson shot the entire trilogy simultaneously in his home country.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lucas directed Star Wars. Nolan directed Inception. Scott directed Gladiator.

questions.question: Which rapper released 'The Slim Shady LP' in 1999, catapulting him to global fame?
questions.explanation_correct: Eminem (Marshall Mathers) won his first Grammy for Best Rap Album with this record.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tupac died in 1996. Snoop Dogg debuted in 1993. Jay-Z is another rap legend.

questions.question: What is the name of the green ogre in the 2001 DreamWorks animated comedy film that won the first Oscar for Best Animated Feature?
questions.explanation_correct: Shrek was a critical and commercial success, voice-acted by Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, and Cameron Diaz.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fiona is the princess. Donkey is his sidekick. Farquaad is the antagonist.

questions.question: Who is the only actor to win three Academy Awards for Best Actor in a Leading Role?
questions.explanation_correct: Daniel Day-Lewis won for My Left Foot (1989), There Will Be Blood (2007), and Lincoln (2012).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jack Nicholson won three Oscars, but one was for Best Supporting Actor. Hanks won two. Hopkins won two.

questions.question: Which British singer-songwriter released the album '21' in 2011, featuring hits like 'Rolling in the Deep'?
questions.explanation_correct: Adele's '21' became the world's best-selling album of the 21st century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are American pop superstars.

questions.question: In which year did the first 'Star Wars' movie (Episode IV: A New Hope) release in theaters?
questions.explanation_correct: Star Wars debuted on May 25, 1977, and became a cultural phenomenon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1980 was The Empire Strikes Back. 1983 was Return of the Jedi.

questions.question: In which fictional Indiana town is the Netflix sci-fi series 'Stranger Things' set?
questions.explanation_correct: Stranger Things is set in the 1983 fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, centered on a government lab.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Riverdale and Twin Peaks are from other drama series. Springfield is from The Simpsons.

questions.question: Which 2009 James Cameron film became the highest-grossing film of all time?
questions.explanation_correct: Avatar grossed over $2.9 billion worldwide, pioneering 3D film technology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Titanic was Cameron's previous record-holder. Avengers: Endgame briefly held the record.

questions.question: Which American singer-songwriter was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016?
questions.explanation_correct: Bob Dylan was awarded the prize 'for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are famous songwriters but did not win the Nobel Prize.

questions.question: From which country does the hit survival drama series 'Squid Game' (2021) originate?
questions.explanation_correct: Squid Game is a South Korean drama created by Hwang Dong-hyuka, becoming Netflix's most-watched series.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other Asian countries did not produce the show.

questions.question: Who played the title character in the Indiana Jones film franchise?
questions.explanation_correct: Harrison Ford played Indiana Jones in five films, from Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) to Dial of Destiny (2023).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sean Connery played his father. Mark Hamill played Luke Skywalker. Cruise is known for Mission: Impossible.

questions.question: Which 1982 Michael Jackson album is the best-selling album of all time?
questions.explanation_correct: Thriller is estimated to have sold over 70 million copies worldwide.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bad and Dangerous were later hits. Off the Wall was his 1979 breakthrough.

questions.question: Which 1994 Disney animated film, featuring music by Elton John, tells the story of a lion cub named Simba?
questions.explanation_correct: The Lion King is one of Disney's most successful animated releases, inspired by Hamlet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bambi is from 1942. The Jungle Book is 1967. Tarzan is 1999.

questions.question: What is the name of the FBI Special Agent who investigates the murder of Laura Palmer in 'Twin Peaks'?
questions.explanation_correct: Agent Dale Cooper (played by Kyle MacLachlan) was sent to Twin Peaks in David Lynch's cult series.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mulder is from The X-Files. Douglas is from Mindhunter. Holmes is a classic detective.

questions.question: Who was the lead singer of the British rock band Queen, who passed away in 1991?
questions.explanation_correct: Freddie Mercury (born Farrokh Bulsara) was known for his flamboyant stage persona and four-octave vocal range.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bowie was a solo artist. George Michael was in Wham! and went solo. Elton John is a solo artist.

questions.question: Who directed the films 'Pulp Fiction', 'Kill Bill', and 'Inglourious Basterds'?
questions.explanation_correct: Quentin Tarantino is known for his stylized violence, pop culture references, and non-linear storylines.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scorsese directed Goodfellas. Nolan directed Inception. Fincher directed Fight Club.

questions.question: Which female artist is known as the 'Queen of Pop', achieving fame in the 1980s with hits like 'Like a Virgin'?
questions.explanation_correct: Madonna became a cultural icon, pushing boundaries in songwriting and music videos.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lauper was her contemporary. Houston was known for her vocals. Cher is a veteran pop icon.

questions.question: Which animation studio produced the first fully computer-animated feature film, 'Toy Story' (1995)?
questions.explanation_correct: Pixar Animation Studios, originally part of Lucasfilm, produced the film, which was distributed by Disney.
questions.explanation_incorrect: DreamWorks was founded in 1994. Ghibli is Japanese. Disney did traditional animation.

questions.question: Who won a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his portrayal of the Joker in 'The Dark Knight' (2008)?
questions.explanation_correct: Heath Ledger passed away in January 2008; his performance as the Joker was widely acclaimed.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nicholson played Joker in 1989. Phoenix played Joker in 2019 (winning Best Actor). Leto played Joker in Suicide Squad.

questions.question: What is the highest prize awarded at the Cannes Film Festival?
questions.explanation_correct: The Palme d'Or was introduced in 1955 as the festival's highest honor.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Golden Lion is Venice. Golden Bear is Berlin. Golden Globe is the Hollywood Foreign Press Association.

questions.question: From which country does the avant-garde pop artist Björk originate?
questions.explanation_correct: Björk was born in Reykjavík, Iceland, starting her career with the band The Sugarcubes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other Nordic countries are not her homeland.

questions.question: What is the name of the Scranton manager in the US version of 'The Office', played by Steve Carell?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Scott is the well-meaning but socially awkward regional manager of Dunder Mifflin Scranton.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dwight is his assistant. Jim is a salesman. Pam is the receptionist.

questions.question: Which Ridley Scott sci-fi movie starring Harrison Ford is a cornerstone of the cyberpunk genre?
questions.explanation_correct: Blade Runner (1982), adapted from Philip K. Dick's novel, depicts a dystopian future of replicants.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alien is a sci-fi horror. Gladiator is a historical epic. Prometheus is a prequel to Alien.

questions.question: Which English rock legend adopted the alien persona Ziggy Stardust in 1972?
questions.explanation_correct: David Bowie created Ziggy Stardust for his landmark album 'The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jagger is the Rolling Stones frontman. John is a pop-rock singer-songwriter. Stewart is a rock singer.

questions.question: Which director won Best Director for the black-and-white Holocaust drama 'Schindler's List' (1993)?
questions.explanation_correct: Steven Spielberg shot the film in Poland, winning Best Picture and Best Director.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Polanski directed The Pianist. Kubrick and Coppola did other acclaimed war/drama films.

questions.question: Which social media platform, launched by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004, became the largest social network in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: Facebook was founded at Harvard University and grew to billions of active monthly users.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Twitter was launched in 2006. Instagram in 2010. MySpace was popular in the early 2000s before Facebook's rise.

questions.question: Which actor plays the character of Wolverine in the X-Men film series?
questions.explanation_correct: Hugh Jackman played Wolverine (Logan) for 17 years, from X-Men (2000) to Logan (2017) and returned in Deadpool & Wolverine (2024).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Stewart played Professor X. McKellen played Magneto. Reynolds plays Deadpool.

questions.question: Which sci-fi anthology series, created by Charlie Brooker, explores the dark side of technology?
questions.explanation_correct: Black Mirror began on Channel 4 in the UK before moving to Netflix, examining modern techno-paranoia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Twilight Zone is a classic anthology. Doctor Who is a time-travel series. Westworld is a serialized drama about AI.

questions.question: Which British band released the best-selling concept album 'The Dark Side of the Moon' in 1973?
questions.explanation_correct: Pink Floyd's progressive rock album stayed on the Billboard charts for a record-breaking 741 weeks.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Led Zeppelin, The Who, and Deep Purple were other prominent rock bands of that era.

questions.question: Which movie won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 2020, becoming the first non-English language film to win the award?
options: Once Upon a Time in Hollywood
questions.explanation_correct: South Korean thriller Parasite, directed by Bong Joon-ho, won four Oscars, including Best Director and Best Picture.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Roma was nominated in 2019 but lost. 1917 and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood were nominees in 2020.

questions.question: Which ancient empire was ruled by the law code known as Hammurabi's Code?
questions.explanation_correct: Hammurabi's Code is one of the oldest deciphered writings of significant length in the world, enacted by the Babylonian king Hammurabi around 1750 BC.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other ancient empires had different legal structures, such as the later Persian satrapies or Egyptian royal decrees.

questions.question: Who was the first woman to be awarded a Nobel Prize, winning it in Physics in 1903?
questions.explanation_correct: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 (shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) and later won in Chemistry in 1911.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Irène Joliot-Curie (Marie's daughter) won in 1935. Rosalind Franklin contributed to DNA structure discovery but did not receive a Nobel. Lise Meitner co-discovered nuclear fission but was bypassed.

questions.question: In which year was King Charles I of England executed, leading to the establishment of a republic under Oliver Cromwell?
questions.explanation_correct: King Charles I was executed on January 30, 1649, following his defeat in the English Civil War, starting the Commonwealth period.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1642 was the start of the Civil War. 1660 was the Restoration of the monarchy under Charles II. 1688 was the Glorious Revolution.

questions.question: In which year did the Meiji Restoration occur, restoring practical imperial rule to Japan under Emperor Meiji?
questions.explanation_correct: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and accelerated Japan's modernization and industrialization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1853 was the arrival of Commodore Perry. 1895 was the end of the First Sino-Japanese War. 1912 was the end of the Meiji era.

questions.question: In which year did Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin become the first human to travel into outer space?
questions.explanation_correct: Yuri Gagarin completed a single orbit of Earth in Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1957 was the launch of Sputnik 1. 1963 was the spaceflight of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space. 1969 was the Apollo 11 Moon landing.

questions.question: In which year did the Battle of Agincourt take place, resulting in a major English victory under Henry V?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Agincourt took place on October 25, 1415, in northern France during the Hundred Years' War.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1346 was the Battle of Crécy. 1356 was the Battle of Poitiers. 1453 was the Battle of Castillon, ending the war.

questions.question: Who was the first Emperor of a unified China, serving as the founder of the Qin dynasty?
questions.explanation_correct: Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC, standardizing writing, currency, and initiating the Great Wall.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Han Wudi was a famous Han dynasty emperor. Tang Taizong co-founded the Tang dynasty. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in the 13th century.

questions.question: In which year did the Suez Crisis occur, following Egypt's nationalization of the Suez Canal?
questions.explanation_correct: The Suez Crisis occurred in late 1956, leading to a military invasion by Israel, the UK, and France, which subsequently withdrew under US and Soviet pressure.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1948 was the Arab-Israeli War. 1967 was the Six-Day War. 1973 was the Yom Kippur War.

questions.question: For how many years did Louis XIV, the 'Sun King', rule France, marking the longest recorded reign of any monarch of a sovereign country?
questions.explanation_correct: Louis XIV ruled France from 1643 to 1715, a total of 72 years and 110 days.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 64 years is close to Queen Victoria's reign (63 years). 50 and 82 years are not matching any major French monarch's reign.

questions.question: Which series of peace treaties signed in 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire?
questions.explanation_correct: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 established the foundations of the modern sovereign state system.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Treaty of Utrecht (1713) ended the Spanish Succession. Peace of Augsburg (1555) allowed princes to select Lutheranism or Catholicism. Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly discovered lands outside Europe.

questions.question: In which year was the League of Nations founded, as a result of the Paris Peace Conference that ended the First World War?
questions.explanation_correct: The League of Nations was formally established on January 10, 1920, with its headquarters in Geneva.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1918 was the end of WWI. 1925 was the Locarno Treaties. 1945 was the founding of the United Nations.

questions.question: Which volcanic island in the Sunda Strait erupted cataclysmically in 1883, creating one of the loudest sounds in recorded history?
questions.explanation_correct: The eruption of Krakatoa in August 1883 destroyed over 70% of the island and was heard up to 3,000 miles away.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tambora erupted in 1815 (causing the Year Without a Summer). Pinatubo erupted in 1991. Pelée erupted in 1902.

questions.question: In which century did the Plague of Justinian first strike the Byzantine Empire and its neighbors, killing millions?
questions.explanation_correct: The Plague of Justinian began around 541 AD, which is in the 6th century, severely weakening the Byzantine Empire.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other centuries do not align with the reign of Emperor Justinian I (527–565 AD).

questions.question: Which English king was forced to accept the Bill of Rights in 1689 following the Glorious Revolution?
questions.explanation_correct: William III (William of Orange) and Mary II accepted the Bill of Rights in 1689, establishing a constitutional monarchy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: James II was deposed in the Glorious Revolution. Charles II ruled prior (1660-1685). George I was the first Hanoverian king (1714).

questions.question: In which year did the English Navy defeat the Spanish Armada sent by Philip II of Spain?
questions.explanation_correct: The Spanish Armada was defeated in August 1588 under the strategic leadership of Lord Howard of Effingham and Sir Francis Drake.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1571 was the Battle of Lepanto. 1605 was the Gunpowder Plot. 1618 was the start of the Thirty Years' War.

questions.question: What was the military code name for the Allied invasion of Sicily in July 1943?
questions.explanation_correct: Operation Husky was a major campaign in which the Allies took Sicily from the Axis powers, facilitating the downfall of Mussolini.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Operation Overlord was the Normandy invasion. Operation Torch was the invasion of French North Africa. Operation Barbarossa was the German invasion of the USSR.

questions.question: Which German archaeologist discovered the remains of ancient Troy in the 1870s at Hisarlik, Turkey?
questions.explanation_correct: Heinrich Schliemann excavated the site of Hisarlik in the 1870s, proving that the legendary city of Troy had a physical location.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arthur Evans excavated Knossos on Crete. Howard Carter discovered Tutankhamun's tomb. Flinders Petrie was a pioneer of systematic methodology in Egyptology.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation_correct: Ottawa was chosen as the capital by Queen Victoria in 1857 due to its location between English and French speaking regions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Toronto is the most populous city. Montreal is the second-most populous. Vancouver is the major hub of Western Canada.

questions.question: Which lake is the deepest in the world, containing more water than all the North American Great Lakes combined?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Baikal in Siberia, Russia, has a maximum depth of 1,642 meters (5,387 ft) and is the world's largest freshwater lake by volume.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tanganyika is the second deepest. Superior is the largest by surface area. Victoria is the largest lake in Africa.

questions.question: What is the largest lake in Africa by surface area?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Victoria is the world's largest tropical lake, shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tanganyika and Malawi are deep rift valley lakes. Lake Chad is shallow and has shrunk dramatically.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Turkey?
questions.explanation_correct: Ankara became the capital of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, succeeding Istanbul after the Turkish War of Independence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Istanbul is the largest city and former Ottoman capital. Izmir and Antalya are other major Turkish cities.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Brazil?
questions.explanation_correct: Brasilia is a planned city inaugurated in 1960, designed by Oscar Niemeyer and Lúcio Costa to move the capital inland.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rio de Janeiro was the capital before 1960. São Paulo is the largest city. Salvador was Brazil's first capital.

questions.question: To which country do the Canary Islands, located off the northwest coast of Africa, belong?
questions.explanation_correct: The Canary Islands are an archipelago that forms an autonomous community of Spain.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Portugal owns Madeira and the Azores. Morocco lies adjacent. France has no claims in the Canary Islands.

questions.question: Which river is the longest in Europe, flowing entirely within Russia into the Caspian Sea?
questions.explanation_correct: The Volga River is approximately 3,530 km (2,193 miles) long and is widely regarded as the national river of Russia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Danube is the second-longest, flowing through Central/Eastern Europe. Rhine is a major Western European river. Ural flows into the Caspian but is shorter.

questions.question: What is the tallest mountain in Europe, located in the Caucasus Range?
questions.explanation_correct: Mount Elbrus is a dormant volcano in Russia rising to 5,642 meters (18,510 ft), making it the highest peak in Europe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mont Blanc (4,810 m) is the highest in the Alps. Matterhorn is a famous alpine peak. Etna is an active volcano in Sicily.

questions.question: Which country has the most natural lakes in the world, containing over 60% of the world's lakes?
questions.explanation_correct: Canada contains more than 879,000 lakes, covering about 9% of the country's total area.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Finland is famous as the 'Land of a Thousand Lakes' but has fewer than Canada. Russia and the US also have many but not as many as Canada.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Morocco?
questions.explanation_correct: Rabat is the capital city, whereas Casablanca is the largest city and economic hub of Morocco.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Casablanca, Marrakesh, and Fes are other historical and populous cities of Morocco.

questions.question: Which cold desert covers parts of northern and northwestern China and southern Mongolia?
questions.explanation_correct: The Gobi Desert is a rain shadow desert formed by the Himalayan range blockading moisture from the Indian Ocean.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Karakum is in Turkmenistan. Taklamakan is in western China. Thar is in India/Pakistan.

questions.question: Which sea, an elongated embayment of the Mediterranean, separates the Greek peninsula from Anatolia (Turkey)?
questions.explanation_correct: The Aegean Sea contains thousands of islands and was the cradle of early Greek civilizations.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Adriatic separates Italy from the Balkans. Ionian lies west of Greece. Tyrrhenian lies west of Italy.

questions.question: What is the de facto capital city of Switzerland?
questions.explanation_correct: Bern is referred to as the 'federal city' of Switzerland, serving as the de facto capital.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zurich is the largest city. Geneva hosts many international organizations. Basel is a cultural and chemical industry center.

questions.question: Which active volcano is located on the east coast of Sicily, Italy?
questions.explanation_correct: Mount Etna is one of the world's most active volcanoes and the highest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vesuvius is near Naples. Stromboli and Vulcano are Aeolian islands north of Sicily.

questions.question: Which country shares the longest international land border with the United States?
questions.explanation_correct: The Canada–United States border is the longest international land border in the world, spanning 8,891 kilometers (5,525 miles).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mexico is the southern neighbor with a shorter border. Russia shares a maritime border. Cuba is an island nation.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Vietnam?
questions.explanation_correct: Hanoi has been the capital since the reunification of North and South Vietnam in 1976.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ho Chi Minh City (formerly Saigon) is the largest city. Da Nang is a major port. Hue was the imperial capital.

questions.question: What is the smallest independent country in the world by both area and population?
questions.explanation_correct: Vatican City covers an area of about 0.49 square kilometers (121 acres) and is surrounded by Rome, Italy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monaco is the second-smallest. Nauru is the smallest island nation. Tuvalu is another tiny island country.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for the element Gold?
questions.explanation_correct: The chemical symbol Au comes from the Latin word for gold, 'aurum', which means 'shining dawn'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ag is silver (argentum). Gd is gadolinium. Go is not a valid chemical symbol.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system has the most confirmed moons as of recent discoveries?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn overtook Jupiter with over 140 confirmed moons, making it the planet with the highest number of satellites.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter was long considered the leader and has over 95 moons. Uranus (28) and Neptune (16) have fewer.

questions.question: Which gas is the most abundant in Earth's atmosphere, making up approximately 78% of it?
questions.explanation_correct: Nitrogen (N2) makes up 78.08% of dry air, followed by Oxygen (20.95%) and Argon (0.93%).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oxygen is the second most abundant. Argon is third. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas making up about 0.04%.

questions.question: Which organelle is commonly referred to as the 'powerhouse of the cell' due to its role in ATP generation?
questions.explanation_correct: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's supply of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), used as a source of chemical energy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The nucleus contains genetic material. Ribosomes assemble proteins. The Golgi apparatus packages proteins.

questions.question: Which Russian chemist is credited with formulating the Periodic Law and creating the first version of the Periodic Table of Elements?
questions.explanation_correct: Mendeleev published the Periodic Table in 1869, organizing elements by atomic mass and leaving gaps for undiscovered ones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lomonosov was an 18th-century polymath. Butlerov made contributions to chemical structure. Legasov was a Soviet inorganic chemist known for the Chernobyl response.

questions.question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, rounded to the nearest thousand kilometers per second?
questions.explanation_correct: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792.458 km/s, which is commonly rounded to 300,000 km/s (or 3x10^8 m/s).
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other numbers are incorrect representations of this fundamental physical constant.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation_correct: The ohm (symbol: Ω) is named after German physicist Georg Ohm, who formulated Ohm's Law.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Volt measures voltage. Ampere measures current. Watt measures power.

questions.question: Which human blood type is considered the 'universal donor' for red blood cells?
questions.explanation_correct: O negative (O-) blood lacks A, B, and Rh antigens, meaning it can be transfused to patients of any blood type in emergencies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: O positive is compatible only with Rh positive types. AB positive is the universal recipient.

questions.question: What is the closest star to the Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: The Sun is the closest star to Earth, at an average distance of about 149.6 million kilometers (1 AU).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Proxima Centauri is the closest star to our solar system, but the Sun is the closest star to Earth itself. Sirius and Alpha Centauri are further.

questions.question: Which organic acid is primarily responsible for the sour taste of lemons and limes?
questions.explanation_correct: Citric acid is a weak organic acid found naturally in citrus fruits, constituting up to 8% of the dry weight of lemons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Acetic acid is in vinegar. Lactic acid is in sour milk/muscles. Malic acid is prominent in apples.

questions.question: What chemical process do green plants use to synthesize nutrients from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight?
questions.explanation_correct: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, releasing oxygen as a byproduct of converting solar energy to chemical energy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Respiration is the breakdown of nutrients. Transpiration is water movement through plants. Fermentation is anaerobic metabolism.

questions.question: What is the name of the Earth's solid outermost chemical layer?
questions.explanation_correct: The crust is the thin outer shell of the Earth, varying in thickness from about 5 km (oceanic) to 70 km (continental).
questions.explanation_incorrect: The mantle is the thick layer below the crust. The outer core is liquid metal. The inner core is solid iron-nickel.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle carries a negative elementary charge?
questions.explanation_correct: Electrons are fundamental particles discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897 that orbit atomic nuclei.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Protons are positively charged. Neutrons have no net charge. Neutrinos are nearly massless, neutral elementary particles.

questions.question: At what temperature does pure water boil at standard atmospheric pressure on the Fahrenheit scale?
questions.explanation_correct: Water boils at 100 °C, which corresponds to 212 °F on the Fahrenheit scale.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 32 °F is the freezing point of water. 100 °F and 180 °F are other temperatures.

questions.question: Which planet is the closest to the Sun in our solar system?
questions.explanation_correct: Mercury orbits the Sun at an average distance of about 57.9 million kilometers, taking just 88 Earth days to complete one orbit.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus is second, Earth is third, and Mars is fourth.

questions.question: Which English physicist formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation in his book 'Principia'?
questions.explanation_correct: Sir Isaac Newton published the 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' in 1687, laying the groundwork for classical mechanics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo laid early foundations of physics. Einstein formulated relativity. Hawking worked on black holes and cosmology.

questions.question: Which gas do humans expel in the greatest concentration when they exhale, aside from nitrogen?
questions.explanation_correct: Exhaled air consists of about 78% nitrogen, 16% oxygen (since the body only absorbs a portion of inhaled oxygen), 4% carbon dioxide, and some water vapor.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Carbon dioxide increases significantly from inhalation (0.04% to 4%) but is still less abundant than oxygen in exhaled breath. Nitrogen is the absolute highest.

questions.question: Which Italian Renaissance master sculpted the famous marble statue of David in Florence?
questions.explanation_correct: Michelangelo created the sculpture between 1501 and 1504, depicting the biblical hero David.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Donatello sculpted an earlier bronze David. Leonardo was a painter/inventor but did not sculpt this statue. Bernini sculpted a baroque David in action.

questions.question: Who wrote the famous tragedy 'Hamlet', telling the story of the Prince of Denmark?
questions.explanation_correct: Hamlet was written by William Shakespeare around 1599–1601 and is his longest play.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Marlowe was a contemporary Elizabethan playwright. Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales. Milton wrote Paradise Lost.

questions.question: Which Dutch Post-Impressionist artist painted 'The Starry Night' while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence?
questions.explanation_correct: Vincent van Gogh painted 'The Starry Night' in June 1889, depicting the view from his asylum window.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rembrandt and Vermeer are Dutch Golden Age masters. Mondrian is a modern abstract painter.

questions.question: Which British author wrote the dystopian novel '1984', introducing concepts like Big Brother and Thoughtcrime?
questions.explanation_correct: George Orwell (pen name of Eric Blair) published '1984' in 1949 as a warning against totalitarianism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Huxley wrote Brave New World. Bradbury wrote Fahrenheit 451. Doyle created Sherlock Holmes.

questions.question: Claude Monet's painting 'Impression, Sunrise' gave its name to which major 19th-century art movement?
questions.explanation_correct: The term 'Impressionism' was coined by an art critic in a hostile review of Monet's painting in 1874.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Expressionism and Cubism are 20th-century movements. Realism preceded Impressionism.

questions.question: Which German composer wrote the Piano Sonata No. 14, commonly known as the 'Moonlight Sonata'?
questions.explanation_correct: Beethoven completed the sonata in 1801, dedicating it to his pupil Countess Giulietta Guicciardi.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bach was a Baroque master. Brahms and Wagner were Romantic era composers.

questions.question: Which American author wrote the 1925 novel 'The Great Gatsby', exploring the excesses of the Jazz Age?
questions.explanation_correct: Fitzgerald's novel captures the decade's materialism, disillusionment, and search for the American Dream.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hemingway, Faulkner, and Steinbeck were other prominent 20th-century American writers.

questions.question: Which English novelist wrote 'Pride and Prejudice', published in 1813?
questions.explanation_correct: Jane Austen wrote 'Pride and Prejudice', depicting the romantic clash between Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Brontë wrote Jane Eyre. Shelley wrote Frankenstein. George Eliot wrote Middlemarch.

questions.question: Which ancient epic poem, attributed to Homer, recounts the events of the final weeks of the Trojan War?
questions.explanation_correct: The Iliad is set during the ten-year siege of Troy, focusing on the wrath of Achilles.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Odyssey recounts Odysseus's journey home. The Aeneid is Roman (Virgil). Gilgamesh is ancient Mesopotamian.

questions.question: Which Italian polymath painted the 'Mona Lisa' and 'The Last Supper' during the High Renaissance?
questions.explanation_correct: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa (La Gioconda) in the early 16th century, using his famous sfumato technique.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Michelangelo was a sculptor/painter (Sistine Chapel). Raphael was a painter (School of Athens). Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus.

questions.question: In which Parisian museum is the ancient Greek statue of Venus de Milo permanently exhibited?
questions.explanation_correct: The Venus de Milo was discovered on the island of Milos in 1820 and is one of the Louvre's most famous works.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Musée d'Orsay houses Impressionist art. Pompidou is modern art. Orangerie houses Monet's Water Lilies.

questions.question: Who wrote the Golden Age Spanish novel 'Don Quixote', widely considered the first modern novel?
questions.explanation_correct: Cervantes published the novel in two parts (1605 and 1615), telling the story of Alonzo Quixano who thinks he is a knight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lope de Vega was a contemporary playwright. Lorca was a 20th-century poet. Márquez was a Colombian novelist (One Hundred Years of Solitude).

questions.question: Which Norwegian Expressionist artist created the famous composition 'The Scream'?
questions.explanation_correct: Munch created four versions of 'The Scream' between 1893 and 1910, representing existential anxiety.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Klimt and Schiele were Austrian symbolists/expressionists. Macke was a German expressionist.

questions.question: Which French sculptor created 'The Thinker', originally conceived as part of a monumental gateway called 'The Gates of Hell'?
questions.explanation_correct: Rodin cast the first small plaster version of 'The Thinker' (Le Penseur) around 1880.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Claudel was his collaborator and sculptor. Degas is known for his Little Dancer statue. Houdon was a neoclassical sculptor.

questions.question: Which child prodigy and classical composer wrote 'The Magic Flute' and 'The Marriage of Figaro' before dying at age 35?
questions.explanation_correct: Mozart composed over 600 works in his short life, including symphonies, concertos, and operas that defined the Classical era.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Schubert, Mendelssohn, and Haydn were other prominent Austrian/German composers of the Classical and early Romantic eras.

questions.question: Which Russian author wrote 'Crime and Punishment', centering on the mental anguish of Raskolnikov?
questions.explanation_correct: Dostoevsky's novel was published in serial parts in 1866, exploring guilt, redemption, and morality.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tolstoy wrote War and Peace. Chekhov was a master of plays and short stories. Turgenev wrote Fathers and Sons.

questions.question: Salvador Dalí and René Magritte are famous exponents of which 20th-century artistic and literary movement?
questions.explanation_correct: Surrealism sought to channel the unconscious mind to unlock the power of imagination, producing dreamlike imagery.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dadaism was an anti-war, anti-art movement that preceded Surrealism. Futurism glorified technology. Abstract Expressionism was post-WWII.

questions.question: Which country won the inaugural FIFA World Cup tournament held in 1930?
questions.explanation_correct: Uruguay hosted the first tournament and defeated Argentina 4-2 in the final in Montevideo.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Argentina were runners-up. Brazil and Italy did not win their first titles until 1958 and 1934 respectively.

questions.question: How many players from each team are allowed on the field at the start of a standard association football (soccer) match?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard soccer match is played between two teams of 11 players each, including one goalkeeper.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The other numbers do not represent standard football team sizes.

questions.question: Which city hosted the Summer Olympic Games in 2012, becoming the first city to host the modern Olympics three times?
questions.explanation_correct: London hosted the Games in 1908, 1948, and 2012.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Athens hosted in 1896 and 2004. Paris hosted in 1900, 1924, and 2024. Los Angeles hosted in 1932, 1984, and is scheduled for 2028.

questions.question: Which sport is played on a court using lightweight rackets and a shuttlecock?
questions.explanation_correct: Badminton involves hitting a feathered or plastic shuttlecock over a high net.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Squash, table tennis, and racquetball are played with balls.

questions.question: Which of the four Grand Slam tennis tournaments is the only one played on natural grass courts?
questions.explanation_correct: Wimbledon, held in London, is the oldest tennis tournament and has maintained grass courts since 1877.
questions.explanation_incorrect: French Open is on clay. Australian and US Opens are played on hard courts.

questions.question: Which American swimmer is the most decorated Olympian of all time, with a total of 28 Olympic medals?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Phelps won 23 gold, 3 silver, and 2 bronze medals across four Olympic Games (2004–2016).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Spitz won 9 golds. Lochte won 12 medals. Thorpe is an Australian swimming legend with 9 medals.

questions.question: What is the standard duration of a professional Rugby Union match, excluding extra time?
questions.explanation_correct: A Rugby Union match consists of two halves of 40 minutes each.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Soccer is 90 minutes. American football and ice hockey are 60 minutes of active game time.

questions.question: In which country did the martial art of Capoeira, which combines elements of dance and acrobatics, originate?
questions.explanation_correct: Capoeira was developed in Brazil by enslaved Africans in the early 16th century as a hidden self-defense mechanism.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Angola was the cultural source for some elements. Portugal was the colonizing power. Cuba is not associated.

questions.question: Which British driver holds the record for the most Formula One Grand Prix wins and shares the record of seven World Championships with Michael Schumacher?
questions.explanation_correct: Lewis Hamilton won his titles between 2008 and 2020, driving for McLaren and Mercedes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vettel won 4 titles. Verstappen won titles in the 2020s. Button won 1 title in 2009.

questions.question: In which Olympic sport do players slide stones on a sheet of ice towards a target and sweep the ice with brooms?
questions.explanation_correct: Curling is nicknamed 'chess on ice' due to the strategic nature of placing the stones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bobsleigh, luge, and skeleton are high-speed sliding track sports.

questions.question: How many points is a standard touchdown worth in American football, before any conversion attempt?
questions.explanation_correct: A touchdown scores 6 points, after which the team can attempt a one-point extra kick or a two-point conversion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 3 is a field goal. 7 is a touchdown with a successful extra point. 2 is a safety.

questions.question: Which country is the origin of the martial art Judo, meaning 'gentle way'?
questions.explanation_correct: Judo was created in Japan in 1882 by Jigoro Kano as a physical, mental, and moral pedagogy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kung Fu originated in China. Taekwondo in Korea. Muay Thai in Thailand.

questions.question: Which major golf tournament is held annually at the Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia?
questions.explanation_correct: The Masters Tournament is the only major golf tournament that is played at the same course every year.
questions.explanation_incorrect: U.S. Open, PGA Championship, and The Open (held in the UK) rotate their venues.

questions.question: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held in 1896?
questions.explanation_correct: The 1896 Games were officially known as the Games of the I Olympiad, held in Athens, Greece.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rome hosted in 1960. Paris in 1900. Olympia was the site of the ancient games.

questions.question: Which legendary NBA player, who led the Chicago Bulls to six championships in the 1990s, was nicknamed 'His Airness'?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Jordan won six Finals MVP awards and is widely considered the greatest basketball player of all time.
questions.explanation_incorrect: LeBron James played primarily in the 21st century. Bryant was star of the Lakers. Johnson led the Lakers in the 1980s.

questions.question: Which nation is the only one to have participated in every single FIFA World Cup tournament since its inception in 1930?
questions.explanation_correct: Brazil has played in all 22 World Cup tournaments and holds the record for the most titles won (five).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Germany, Italy, and Argentina have missed or failed to qualify for some editions.

questions.question: Who directed the 2014 science fiction film 'Interstellar', starring Matthew McConaughey?
questions.explanation_correct: Christopher Nolan directed and co-wrote the film, which was praised for its scientific accuracy regarding black holes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Villeneuve directed Dune and Arrival. Scott directed Alien and Blade Runner. Cameron directed Avatar.

questions.question: What is the hacker alias of Thomas Anderson, played by Keanu Reeves, in the sci-fi franchise 'The Matrix'?
questions.explanation_correct: Thomas Anderson goes by the handle 'Neo' online and is prophesied to be 'The One' who will free humanity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Morpheus is his mentor. Agent Smith is the main antagonist. Cypher is a member who betrays the crew.

questions.question: Which British rock band recorded and released the epic six-minute song 'Bohemian Rhapsody' in 1975?
questions.explanation_correct: Bohemian Rhapsody was written by Freddie Mercury for the album 'A Night at the Opera', topping charts worldwide.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Led Zeppelin, The Who, and Pink Floyd were other massive British bands but had no role in this song.

questions.question: Which James Cameron film, released in 2009, is the highest-grossing film of all time (unadjusted for inflation)?
questions.explanation_correct: Avatar grossed over $2.9 billion worldwide, pioneering 3D technology.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Endgame is second. Titanic is third. The Force Awakens is fifth.

questions.question: What is the name of the fictional continent where the majority of the action in 'Game of Thrones' takes place?
questions.explanation_correct: Westeros is home to the Seven Kingdoms, while Essos is the continent to the east.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Essos is the eastern continent. Tamriel is from The Elder Scrolls. Middle-earth is J.R.R. Tolkien's universe.

questions.question: Which animation studio produced 'Toy Story' in 1995, the first feature-length computer-animated film?
questions.explanation_correct: Pixar produced Toy Story in partnership with Disney, launching a new era of animation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: DreamWorks was founded in 1994 and released Antz in 1998. Disney distributed but didn't animate it. Ghibli is a Japanese hand-drawn studio.

questions.question: Which American singer-songwriter, who released the albums 'Thriller' and 'Bad', is known as the 'King of Pop'?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' (1982) remains the best-selling album of all time, with estimated sales of over 70 million copies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Prince was Jackson's rival. Presley is the 'King of Rock and Roll'. Stevie Wonder is a soul/pop icon.

questions.question: Which critically acclaimed TV drama stars Bryan Cranston as Walter White, a high school chemistry teacher who turns to cooking methamphetamine?
questions.explanation_correct: Breaking Bad aired for five seasons on AMC, winning 16 Primetime Emmy Awards.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Better Call Saul is a prequel spin-off. Mad Men is about 1960s advertising. The Wire is a police drama set in Baltimore.

questions.question: What is the name of the school of witchcraft and wizardry attended by Harry Potter?
questions.explanation_correct: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry is located in Scotland and was founded by four legendary wizards.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Durmstrang and Beauxbatons are European wizarding schools. Ilvermorny is the American school.

questions.question: Which actor played the lead character Jack Dawson in the 1997 disaster-romance movie 'Titanic'?
questions.explanation_correct: Leonardo DiCaprio starred alongside Kate Winslet in James Cameron's record-breaking film.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pitt, Depp, and Damon were considered for roles or were stars of other major 90s films but not Titanic.

questions.question: Which iconic English band, featuring John Lennon and Paul McCartney, was nicknamed the 'Fab Four'?
questions.explanation_correct: The Beatles formed in Liverpool in 1960 and became the most influential band in popular music history.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rolling Stones, Kinks, and Who were other bands of the British Invasion.

questions.question: Which actor portrayed Tony Stark / Iron Man in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, starting with the 2008 film 'Iron Man'?
questions.explanation_correct: Robert Downey Jr.'s portrayal of Iron Man kicked off the MCU and concluded in Avengers: Endgame (2019).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Evans played Captain America. Hemsworth plays Thor. Ruffalo plays Bruce Banner/Hulk.

questions.question: Who wrote and directed the 1994 independent neo-noir crime film 'Pulp Fiction'?
questions.explanation_correct: Pulp Fiction won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival and won Tarantino an Oscar for Best Original Screenplay.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scorsese directed Goodfellas. Coen Brothers directed Fargo. Fincher directed Fight Club.

questions.question: In which country did the pop group ABBA, known for hits like 'Dancing Queen' and 'Mamma Mia', form in 1972?
questions.explanation_correct: ABBA formed in Stockholm, Sweden, and won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974 with 'Waterloo'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other Nordic countries are not the origin of ABBA.

questions.question: Who was the original voice actor of Mickey Mouse when the character debuted in 'Steamboat Willie' in 1928?
questions.explanation_correct: Walt Disney voiced Mickey Mouse from 1928 until 1947, when the task was passed to Jimmy Macdonald.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ub Iwerks co-created Mickey. Mel Blanc voiced Looney Tunes characters. Clarence Nash voiced Donald Duck.

questions.question: Which animated sea sponge, created by Stephen Hillenburg, lives in a pineapple under the sea in Bikini Bottom?
questions.explanation_correct: SpongeBob SquarePants has aired on Nickelodeon since 1999, becoming one of the most successful media franchises.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patrick is a starfish. Squidward is an octopus. Sandy is a squirrel.

questions.question: Which Babylonian king is credited with creating one of the earliest and most complete written legal codes in ancient history?
questions.explanation_correct: Hammurabi ruled Babylon from 1792 to 1750 BC and established the Code of Hammurabi, consisting of 282 laws scaled on a basalt stele.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens. Sargon founded the Akkadian Empire. Gilgamesh is a legendary hero and king of Uruk.

questions.question: Which battle in 1187 saw Saladin decisively defeat the Crusader forces, leading to the Muslim recapture of Jerusalem?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Hattin occurred on July 4, 1187, where Saladin's forces trapped and destroyed the Crusader army under Guy of Lusignan.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arsuf was a battle won by Richard the Lionheart. Acre was a famous siege. Manzikert (1071) was a Seljuk victory over Byzantium.

questions.question: In which year did Scottish physician Alexander Fleming discover penicillin, the world's first effective antibiotic?
questions.explanation_correct: Fleming discovered penicillin in September 1928 after noticing mold (Penicillium notatum) had killed bacteria in a petri dish in his lab.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1918 was the end of WWI. 1935 was when Prontosil (a sulfa drug) was introduced. 1945 was when Fleming shared the Nobel Prize.

questions.question: What was the name of the flagship of the notorious pirate Blackbeard, which ran aground in North Carolina in 1718?
questions.explanation_correct: Queen Anne's Revenge was originally a French slave ship named La Concorde, captured by Blackbeard in 1717 and heavily armed.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Golden Hind was Francis Drake's ship. Royal Fortune was Bartholomew Roberts' flagship. Adventure Galley was William Kidd's ship.

questions.question: Who was the first woman to travel into space, orbiting the Earth 48 times in June 1963?
questions.explanation_correct: Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova flew aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963, remaining the only woman to fly solo in space.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sally Ride was the first American woman in space (1983). Savitskaya was the second woman (1982). Jemison was the first Black woman (1992).

questions.question: The overthrow of Maximilien Robespierre in July 1794, ending the Reign of Terror, is known by which name?
questions.explanation_correct: The Thermidorian Reaction occurred in the month of Thermidor according to the French Republican Calendar, leading to Robespierre's execution.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Directory was established afterwards. The Coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 was when Napoleon Bonaparte seized power.

questions.question: At which battle in 216 BC did Hannibal surround and destroy a much larger Roman army, considered a tactical masterpiece?
questions.explanation_correct: At Cannae, Hannibal used a double-envelopment tactic to surround and slaughter up to 70,000 Roman soldiers under the consuls Varro and Paullus.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zama (202 BC) was the battle where Scipio defeated Hannibal. Trebia (218 BC) and Trasimene (217 BC) were earlier Carthaginian victories.

questions.question: In which German city did Johannes Gutenberg print his famous 42-Line Bible in the 1450s?
questions.explanation_correct: Gutenberg set up his workshop and printed his movable-type Bible in Mainz, Germany, which revolutionized printing in Europe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Frankfurt became a printing hub later. Cologne and Nuremberg had printing presses established in the following decades.

questions.question: Which desert battle in late 1942 marked a major turning point in the North African Campaign, halting the Axis advance into Egypt?
questions.explanation_correct: The Second Battle of El Alamein saw the British Eighth Army under Bernard Montgomery defeat Erwin Rommel's Panzer Army Africa.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tobruk was besieged earlier. Kasserine Pass was a battle in Tunisia (1943). Gazala was an Axis victory in mid-1942.

questions.question: What is the largest tropical lake in the world, bordered by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake by area and the world's largest tropical lake, named after Queen Victoria.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tanganyika is the world's longest freshwater lake. Malawi is another Rift Valley lake. Chad is a shallow, endorheic lake.

questions.question: Which planned city was inaugurated as the federal capital of Brazil in 1960, replacing Rio de Janeiro?
questions.explanation_correct: Brasília was designed by Oscar Niemeyer and Lúcio Costa in 1956 to move the capital inland, opening officially in April 1960.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rio de Janeiro was the capital before 1960. Salvador was Brazil's first capital. Belo Horizonte was another planned state capital.

questions.question: The cataclysmic eruption of which volcanic island in the Sunda Strait in 1883 generated the loudest sound ever recorded in modern history?
questions.explanation_correct: The August 1883 eruption of Krakatoa shattered the island and created a sound wave heard 3,000 miles away.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD. Pinatubo erupted in 1991. Tambora erupted in 1815, causing the 'Year Without a Summer' (the largest eruption).

questions.question: Which two countries are the only landlocked nations in South America?
questions.explanation_correct: Bolivia lost its coastline in the War of the Pacific. Paraguay is situated deep in the interior, with river access to the Atlantic.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ecuador, Uruguay, Peru, and Chile all have direct ocean coastlines.

questions.question: Which body of water is the only sea on Earth that has no land boundaries, defined instead by ocean currents?
questions.explanation_correct: The Sargasso Sea is located in the North Atlantic Ocean and is bounded by four currents forming an ocean gyre.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Caribbean, Mediterranean, and Red seas are all bounded by mainland coasts and island chains.

questions.question: Which archipelagic province of Ecuador in the Pacific Ocean is famous for its unique wildlife that inspired Charles Darwin's theory of evolution?
questions.explanation_correct: Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands in 1835 aboard HMS Beagle, studying giant tortoises and finches.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Easter Island belongs to Chile. Falkland Islands are a British territory. Juan Fernández Islands belong to Chile.

questions.question: What is the name of the coastal desert in South America that is widely considered the driest non-polar desert in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: The Atacama Desert in Chile receives almost no precipitation due to the rain shadow of the Andes and the Humboldt Current.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Patagonian Desert is in Argentina. Mojave is in the US. Kalahari is a large semi-arid sandy savanna in southern Africa.

questions.question: What is the longest river entirely located within the European continent?
questions.explanation_correct: The Volga River flows through Russia over 3,530 kilometers (2,193 miles) and drains into the Caspian Sea.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Danube is the second-longest. Rhine is a major western river. Ural flows through Russia and Kazakhstan and marks the border.

questions.question: Which waterfall, located in Venezuela, is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall with a height of 979 meters?
questions.explanation_correct: Angel Falls (Kerepakupai Meru) drops from a tabletop mountain (tepui) in the Canaima National Park.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tugela Falls in South Africa is the second tallest. Niagara and Victoria are famous for volume but are much shorter.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system has the shortest day, completing a full rotation on its axis in under 10 hours?
questions.explanation_correct: Jupiter has a rotational period of approximately 9 hours and 56 minutes, despite being the largest planet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Saturn takes about 10.7 hours. Mercury takes 59 Earth days. Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once.

questions.question: Which chemical element is the only metal that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation_correct: Mercury (Hg), historically called quicksilver, remains liquid down to -38.83 °C due to its unique electron configuration.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Gallium and Cesium melt slightly above room temp. Bromine is a liquid at room temp, but it is a nonmetal.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body, accounting for about 16% of body weight?
questions.explanation_correct: The skin (integumentary system) serves as the primary barrier against the external environment and is the largest organ.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Liver is the largest internal organ. Brain and Small Intestine are also large, but smaller than skin.

questions.question: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum, rounded to the nearest thousand kilometers per second?
questions.explanation_correct: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792.458 kilometers per second (about 186,282 miles per second).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other values are mathematically incorrect orders of magnitude.

questions.question: Which American seismologist and physicist co-developed the magnitude scale used to measure the energy released by earthquakes in 1935?
questions.explanation_correct: Charles Richter, along with Beno Gutenberg, developed the Richter magnitude scale in 1935 at Caltech.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mercalli developed the intensity scale based on damage. Reid proposed elastic-rebound theory. Lehmann discovered Earth's inner core.

questions.question: Which chemical element is the most abundant element in the universe, constituting roughly 75% of all baryonic mass?
questions.explanation_correct: Hydrogen (H) is the simplest and most abundant element, forming in massive quantities during the early universe.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Helium is the second most abundant (~24%). Oxygen and Carbon are much rarer, though common on Earth.

questions.question: Which English scientist formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation in his 1687 work 'Principia'?
questions.explanation_correct: Sir Isaac Newton's 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' laid the foundations for classical mechanics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Galileo studied kinematics. Einstein formulated relativity. Kepler formulated the laws of planetary motion.

questions.question: Which two scientists are famously credited with discovering the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953?
questions.explanation_correct: Watson and Crick published their double-helix model of DNA in April 1953, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction data.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mendel founded genetics. Pasteur and Koch studied microbiology. The Curies researched radioactivity.

questions.question: Which Dutch Post-Impressionist painter created the famous masterpiece 'The Starry Night' in 1889 while in an asylum?
questions.explanation_correct: Van Gogh painted 'The Starry Night' from his window at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monet was French. Rembrandt and Vermeer were Dutch Golden Age painters who lived in the 17th century.

questions.question: Which tragedy by William Shakespeare tells the story of a prince of Denmark seeking revenge for his father's murder?
questions.explanation_correct: Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play, set in Denmark, detailing the Prince's plot to avenge the murder of King Hamlet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Macbeth is set in Scotland. King Lear is set in ancient Britain. Othello is set in Venice and Cyprus.

questions.question: Which Italian Baroque composer wrote the set of four violin concertos known as 'The Four Seasons'?
questions.explanation_correct: Vivaldi composed 'The Four Seasons' (Le quattro stagioni) around 1720, depicting spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bach and Handel were German Baroque composers. Monteverdi was an early Italian Baroque pioneer.

questions.question: Which Renaissance master sculpted the marble statues of 'David' and 'Pieta'?
questions.explanation_correct: Michelangelo Buonarroti sculpted the 'Pieta' in Rome before turning 25, and completed 'David' in Florence in 1504.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Donatello sculpted an earlier bronze David. Da Vinci was primarily a painter/inventor. Bernini was a Baroque sculptor.

questions.question: What is the primary building material used for the exterior of the Taj Mahal in India?
questions.explanation_correct: The Taj Mahal is clad in white Makrana marble, which was transported from Rajasthan and is inlaid with semi-precious stones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Red sandstone was used for the surrounding gateway and mosque. Granite and Limestone were not primary materials.

questions.question: Which Colombian author won the Nobel Prize in Literature and is famous for his 1967 novel 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'?
questions.explanation_correct: Márquez pioneered the literary style of magical realism and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vargas Llosa is Peruvian. Borges was Argentinian. Neruda was a Chilean poet.

questions.question: Which French philosopher coined the famous philosophical statement 'Cogito, ergo sum' (I think, therefore I am) in 1637?
questions.explanation_correct: Descartes published this proposition in his 'Discourse on the Method', establishing a foundation for rationalist philosophy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rousseau and Voltaire were Enlightenment figures. Pascal was a mathematician/philosopher who wrote 'Pensées'.

questions.question: Which French painter's 1872 work 'Impression, Sunrise' gave the Impressionist art movement its name?
questions.explanation_correct: Monet's painting of the harbor of Le Havre was criticized by Louis Leroy, who coined the term 'Impressionist' in derision.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Renoir, Manet, and Degas were also associated with the movement, but Monet's work was the direct namesake.

questions.question: Which country's national team has won the most FIFA World Cup titles, with five victories?
questions.explanation_correct: Brazil won the FIFA World Cup in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002, and is the only nation to play in every tournament.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Germany and Italy have four titles each. Argentina has three titles (most recently in 2022).

questions.question: Which country won the first-ever FIFA World Cup tournament held in 1930?
questions.explanation_correct: Uruguay defeated Argentina 4-2 in the final in Montevideo to win the inaugural World Cup.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Argentina was the runner-up. Brazil and Italy did not make the final (Italy didn't even participate).

questions.question: As of 2026, which male tennis player holds the record for the most Grand Slam singles titles in history?
questions.explanation_correct: Novak Djokovic has won 24 Grand Slam singles titles, surpassing Rafael Nadal (22) and Roger Federer (20).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nadal and Federer are behind Djokovic. Sampras retired with 14 titles.

questions.question: Which player became the NBA's all-time leading scorer in February 2023, breaking Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's long-standing record?
questions.explanation_correct: LeBron James broke Abdul-Jabbar's record of 38,387 points on February 7, 2023, while playing for the Los Angeles Lakers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Michael Jordan is 5th. Kobe Bryant is 4th. Karl Malone is 3rd.

questions.question: What color jersey is awarded to the leader of the general classification in the Tour de France?
questions.explanation_correct: The yellow jersey (maillot jaune) represents the overall leader, chosen originally to match the yellow paper of L'Auto newspaper.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Green is for points classification. Polka Dot is for King of the Mountains. White is for best young rider.

questions.question: Who is the Jamaican sprinter who set the men's 100 meters world record of 9.58 seconds in 2009?
questions.explanation_correct: Usain Bolt set the 100m world record of 9.58s at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin on August 16, 2009.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tyson Gay and Yohan Blake have hit 9.69s. Powell held the record before Bolt with 9.74s.

questions.question: How many players are on the field at one time for a single team in defensive play in a standard baseball game?
questions.explanation_correct: A defensive baseball team consists of 9 players: pitcher, catcher, four infielders, and three outfielders.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cricket has 11 players. American football has 11. Other numbers are typical for other sports.

questions.question: Which two drivers share the record for the most Formula One World Drivers' Championships, with seven titles each?
options: Sebastian Vettel and Juan Manuel Fangio
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Schumacher won his 7th title in 2004, and Lewis Hamilton matched him in 2020.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Fangio has 5 titles. Vettel and Prost have 4 titles. Senna has 3 titles. Verstappen has 3 (as of 2023).

questions.question: Which American film director is famous for directing 'Jaws', 'E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial', and 'Schindler's List'?
questions.explanation_correct: Steven Spielberg is one of the most commercially successful directors in history, winning Best Director for 'Schindler's List' and 'Saving Private Ryan'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Scorsese directed 'Goodfellas'. Coppola directed 'The Godfather'. Lucas created 'Star Wars'.

questions.question: Which sandbox block-building game, developed by Mojang and released in 2011, is the best-selling video game of all time?
questions.explanation_correct: Minecraft has sold over 300 million copies across all platforms, allowing players to build and explore infinite 3D worlds.
questions.explanation_incorrect: GTA V is second (~190 million). Tetris has sold around 100 million copies. Wii Sports is the best-selling single-platform game.

questions.question: Created by Matt Groening, what is the longest-running American animated sitcom, debuting as a half-hour show in 1989?
questions.explanation_correct: The Simpsons debuted in December 1989 and has aired over 750 episodes, depicting working-class family life in Springfield.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Family Guy started in 1999. South Park started in 1997. King of the Hill ran from 1997 to 2010.

questions.question: Which 2009 science fiction film directed by James Cameron remains the highest-grossing film of all time (unadjusted for inflation)?
questions.explanation_correct: Avatar grossed over $2.9 billion worldwide, pioneering 3D film technology and set on the alien moon Pandora.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Endgame is second. Titanic is third. The Force Awakens is fourth.

questions.question: Which American singer-songwriter is widely referred to as the 'King of Pop' and released the best-selling album of all time, 'Thriller'?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' (1982) sold an estimated 70 million copies globally. He was an influential figure in dance and fashion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Elvis Presley is the 'King of Rock and Roll'. Prince and Stevie Wonder are other prominent music legends.

questions.question: Which iconic fictional character did Harrison Ford portray in the original 'Star Wars' trilogy, beginning in 1977?
questions.explanation_correct: Harrison Ford played the cynical smuggler Han Solo, captain of the Millennium Falcon.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Luke Skywalker was played by Mark Hamill. Indiana Jones and Rick Deckard (Blade Runner) are other roles of Ford's, not in Star Wars.

questions.question: Which American comic book writer co-created iconic characters like Spider-Man, Iron Man, and the X-Men with artist Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby?
questions.explanation_correct: Stan Lee was the editor-in-chief of Marvel Comics, introducing complex, flawed heroes to the medium.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bob Kane co-created Batman. Jerry Siegel co-created Superman. Jack Kirby was the artist co-creator, not primary writer.

questions.question: Which English rock band released the landmark 1973 concept album 'The Dark Side of the Moon', which charted for a record 741 weeks?
questions.explanation_correct: Pink Floyd's progressive rock album explored themes of conflict, greed, time, and mental illness, utilizing advanced studio techniques.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Led Zeppelin, The Beatles, and Queen did not record this album.

questions.question: In which year did the Panama Canal officially open to maritime traffic, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans?
questions.explanation_correct: The Panama Canal was completed and opened in August 1914, greatly shortening the shipping route between the two oceans.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1904 was when the US took over construction. 1920 was the official formal inauguration ceremony. 1899 was during French attempts.

questions.question: Which female pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty built the famous Djeser-Djeseru temple at Deir el-Bahari and ruled as a male king?
questions.explanation_correct: Hatshepsut reigned from c. 1478 BC, depicting herself as a male pharaoh to legitimize her rule and establishing prosperous trade routes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nefertiti was a queen consort of Akhenaten. Cleopatra VII was of the Ptolemaic dynasty. Sobekneferu was of the 12th Dynasty.

questions.question: Which peace treaty signed in 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic?
