questions.explanation_correct: The Peace of Westphalia established the concept of state sovereignty and co-existence, shaping modern international diplomacy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Utrecht ended the Spanish Succession (1713). Augsburg resolved religious conflict in HRE (1555). Tordesillas divided lands between Spain and Portugal (1494).

questions.question: In which year was US President Abraham Lincoln assassinated by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre?
questions.explanation_correct: President Lincoln was shot on April 14, 1865, just days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, and died the next morning.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1861 was the start of the Civil War. 1863 was the Gettysburg Address. 1870 was during the Reconstruction Era.

questions.question: On which Mediterranean island was Napoleon Bonaparte born in 1769, shortly after the island was purchased by France from Genoa?
questions.explanation_correct: Napoleon was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, to a family of minor Italian nobility, and grew up speaking Italian and Corsican.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Elba was his first place of exile. Saint Helena was his final exile. Sardinia is a neighboring island that remained Italian.

questions.question: Which battle fought in 1916 was the longest and one of the bloodiest of World War I, becoming a symbol of determination for France?
questions.explanation_correct: The Battle of Verdun lasted 303 days from February to December 1916, causing over 700,000 casualties for French and German armies.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Somme was a joint British-French offensive. Marne halted the initial German advance. Gallipoli took place in the Ottoman Empire.

questions.question: Who was the first human in space, completing a single orbit of the Earth in his Vostok 1 spacecraft in April 1961?
questions.explanation_correct: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin made his historic flight on April 12, 1961, launching the era of human spaceflight.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Shepard was the first American in space (suborbital). Glenn was the first American to orbit. Leonov conducted the first spacewalk.

questions.question: Which British monarch reigned for 63 years and 7 months from 1837 to 1901, presiding over the height of the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation_correct: Queen Victoria's reign defined the Victorian Era, marked by great expansion of the British Empire and industrialization.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Elizabeth I ruled in the Tudor era. Anne was the first monarch of Great Britain. Elizabeth II ruled for 70 years (1952-2022).

questions.question: What is the name of the deepest known point in the Earth's oceans, located in the western Pacific Ocean?
questions.explanation_correct: Challenger Deep, located in the Mariana Trench, has a depth of approximately 10,928 meters (35,853 feet).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Java and Sunda trenches are in the Indian Ocean. Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest in the Atlantic.

questions.question: Which country is the most populous nation on the African continent, with a population exceeding 200 million?
questions.explanation_correct: Nigeria has the largest population in Africa, driven by a high fertility rate and a large youth demographic.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ethiopia is the second-most populous. Egypt is third. South Africa has around 60 million people.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada, located at the confluence of several major rivers in Ontario?
questions.explanation_correct: Ottawa was selected as the capital by Queen Victoria in 1857 due to its secure inland location and bilingual region.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Toronto is Canada's largest city. Montreal is the second-largest and largest in Quebec. Vancouver is on the west coast.

questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, is located off the coast of which Australian state?
questions.explanation_correct: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the coast of Queensland in the Coral Sea, consisting of over 2,900 individual reefs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: New South Wales is further south. Western Australia has the Ningaloo Reef. Victoria is in the southeastern corner.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain peak in the Americas, located in the Andes mountain range in Argentina?
questions.explanation_correct: Aconcagua rises to an elevation of 6,961 meters (22,838 feet) above sea level, making it the highest peak outside Asia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Denali (formerly McKinley) is the highest in North America. Chimborazo is the point furthest from the Earth's center.

questions.question: Which lake in Siberia is the world's deepest and oldest freshwater lake, containing about 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater?
questions.explanation_correct: Lake Baikal is 1,642 meters (5,387 feet) deep and formed as an ancient rift valley over 25 million years ago.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area. Tanganyika is the second deepest. Caspian Sea is saline.

questions.question: Which European nation has the highest number of islands in the world, with over 220,000 recorded islands?
questions.explanation_correct: Sweden has approximately 267,570 islands, though only a small fraction are inhabited. Norway is second with over 239,000.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Greece has about 6,000 islands. Indonesia is the largest archipelagic state but has only around 17,000 islands.

questions.question: Which river flows directly through the center of London, England, before emptying into the North Sea?
questions.explanation_correct: The River Thames is England's longest river, serving as a key transport and water resource throughout London's history.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Seine flows through Paris. Danube flows through Central and Eastern Europe. Mersey flows through Liverpool.

questions.question: Who was awarded the first-ever Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for his discovery of X-rays?
questions.explanation_correct: German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays (Röntgen rays) in 1895, revolutionizing medical diagnosis.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Becquerel co-won in 1903 for radioactivity. Planck won in 1918 for quantum theory. Einstein won in 1921 for the photoelectric effect.

questions.question: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system, with surface temperatures exceeding 450 °C due to a runaway greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation_correct: Venus has a dense atmosphere composed mostly of carbon dioxide, which traps heat and makes it hotter than Mercury despite being further from the Sun.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mercury has no atmosphere to retain heat. Mars is very cold. Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface.

questions.question: What is the pH level of chemically pure, neutral water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation_correct: A pH of 7 represents absolute neutrality, where the concentration of hydrogen ions equals hydroxide ions.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 0 is highly acidic. 14 is highly alkaline. 5.5 is typical for slightly acidic rainwater.

questions.question: Which double-membrane organelle is commonly referred to as the 'powerhouse of the cell' due to its role in producing ATP?
questions.explanation_correct: Mitochondria perform cellular respiration, converting nutrients into adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the chemical energy of the cell.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ribosomes synthesize proteins. Golgi apparatus modifies proteins. Lysosomes break down waste products.

questions.question: Which human blood type is considered the 'universal donor' because its red blood cells lack A, B, and Rh antigens?
questions.explanation_correct: O Negative (O-) blood can be transfused to patients of any blood type in emergencies without triggering an immune reaction.
questions.explanation_incorrect: O Positive contains Rh factor. AB Positive is the universal recipient. AB Negative can only donate to AB types.

questions.question: Which diatomic gas is the most abundant in the Earth's atmosphere, making up approximately 78% of its volume?
questions.explanation_correct: Nitrogen (N2) is an inert gas that dilutes oxygen, preventing rapid combustion and supporting biological nitrogen fixation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Oxygen is second (~21%). Argon is third (~0.93%). Carbon Dioxide is a trace gas (~0.04%).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric current, named after a French physicist who was a founder of electromagnetism?
questions.explanation_correct: The Ampere (A), named after André-Marie Ampère, measures the rate of flow of electric charge.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Volt measures potential difference. Ohm measures resistance. Watt measures power.

questions.question: What is the name of the thinnest, outermost solid layer of the Earth, lying above the mantle?
questions.explanation_correct: The Earth's crust ranges from 5 km (oceanic) to 70 km (continental) in thickness and is composed of silicate rocks.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Asthenosphere is highly viscous mantle. Outer Core is liquid iron-nickel. Lithosphere includes crust and upper mantle.

questions.question: Which barred spiral galaxy is the closest major galaxy to our Milky Way, located about 2.5 million light-years away?
questions.explanation_correct: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is the largest member of the Local Group and is on a collision course with the Milky Way.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Triangulum is third-largest. Magellanic Clouds are dwarf satellite galaxies. Whirlpool is a distant grand-design spiral.

questions.question: Which French sculptor created the famous bronze figure 'The Thinker' in 1902, originally part of 'The Gates of Hell'?
questions.explanation_correct: Rodin designed 'The Thinker' (Le Penseur) representing Dante contemplating his work, and it was cast as an independent bronze.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Claudel was his collaborator. Degas sculpted 'Little Dancer'. Giacometti is famous for thin, elongated figures.

questions.question: Which Norwegian expressionist artist painted 'The Scream' in 1893, representing the anxiety of the modern human?
questions.explanation_correct: Munch created four versions of 'The Scream' in paint and pastels, depicting a figure with an agonized expression against a red sky.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Klimt was Austrian symbolist. Schiele was Austrian expressionist. Kandinsky was a Russian abstract pioneer.

questions.question: Which American author wrote the classic 1925 novel 'The Great Gatsby', detailing the excess of the Jazz Age?
questions.explanation_correct: Fitzgerald's 'The Great Gatsby' explores themes of decadence, social upheaval, and the disillusionment of the American Dream.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hemingway wrote 'Farewell to Arms'. Faulkner wrote 'The Sound and the Fury'. Steinbeck wrote 'Grapes of Wrath'.

questions.question: Which Spanish author wrote 'Don Quixote' (published in two parts in 1605 and 1615), considered the first modern novel?
questions.explanation_correct: Cervantes wrote the classic tale of the delusional knight Don Quixote of La Mancha and his squire Sancho Panza.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lope de Vega was a playwright. Lorca was a 20th-century poet. Márquez is Colombian, not Spanish.

questions.question: Which German composer wrote the famous 'Symphony No. 9' (including the 'Ode to Joy') while completely deaf?
questions.explanation_correct: Beethoven premiered his Ninth Symphony in Vienna in 1824, incorporating vocal soloists and a chorus into a symphonic structure.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mozart died young, writing 41 symphonies. Brahms and Schubert lived in the romantic era and were influenced by Beethoven.

questions.question: Which Spanish Cubist artist painted the massive anti-war mural 'Guernica' in 1937 following the bombing of a Basque town?
questions.explanation_correct: Picasso painted 'Guernica' for the Spanish Pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exposition to protest the violence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dalí was a surrealist. Miró was an abstractionist. Goya painted anti-war art in the 19th century ('The Third of May').

questions.question: What is the title of the ancient Greek epic poem attributed to Homer that narrates the events of the final weeks of the Trojan War?
questions.explanation_correct: The Iliad focuses on the rage of Achilles during the tenth year of the siege of Troy.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Odyssey recounts Odysseus' return home. The Aeneid was written in Latin by Virgil. Gilgamesh is Babylonian.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher was the tutor of Alexander the Great and founded the Peripatetic school at the Lyceum?
questions.explanation_correct: Aristotle was a student of Plato who went on to tutor the young Alexander of Macedon in Athens, writing on logic and ethics.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Plato was Aristotle's teacher. Socrates was Plato's teacher. Epicurus founded Epicureanism.

questions.question: Which iconic iron lattice tower was designed by the company of Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris?
questions.explanation_correct: The Eiffel Tower was built as the entrance arch to the 1889 World's Fair, celebrating the centennial of the French Revolution.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arc de Triomphe was built in the early 19th century. Louvre Pyramid was built in 1989. Sacré-Cœur was completed in 1914.

questions.question: Which annual tennis tournament, founded in 1877, is the oldest in the world and the only Grand Slam played on grass?
questions.explanation_correct: Wimbledon is held at the All England Club in London and is known for its strict white dress code for players.
questions.explanation_incorrect: US Open is played on hard courts. French Open is on clay. Australian Open is on hard courts.

questions.question: How many holes are played in a standard, complete round of professional championship golf?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard golf course consists of 18 holes, which players complete in a single round of play.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 9 is a half-round. 36 is two rounds. 72 is the total holes in a standard four-day tournament.

questions.question: What is the name of the trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff champion?
questions.explanation_correct: The Stanley Cup is the oldest professional sports trophy in North America, donated by Lord Stanley of Preston in 1892.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lombardi is for NFL. O'Brien is for NBA. Commissioner's Trophy is for MLB.

questions.question: How many rings are featured on the official Olympic flag, representing the five inhabited continents?
questions.explanation_correct: The Olympic flag has five interlocking rings (blue, yellow, black, green, and red) designed by Pierre de Coubertin in 1913.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other numbers do not correspond to the continents represented.

questions.question: What is the duration in minutes of a standard professional association football match, excluding extra time and halftime?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard football match consists of two halves of 45 minutes each, separated by a 15-minute halftime interval.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 80 minutes is for rugby union. 120 minutes is the total duration if extra time is played.

questions.question: What is the name of the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), played on the first Sunday of February?
questions.explanation_correct: The Super Bowl was created as part of the merger agreement between the NFL and AFL, first played in January 1967.
questions.explanation_incorrect: World Series is baseball's championship. Grey Cup is CFL. Pro Bowl is the NFL all-star game.

questions.question: What is the official distance of a standard marathon race in kilometers, based on the 1908 London Olympics distance?
questions.explanation_correct: The marathon distance was standardized at 42.195 km (26 miles 385 yards) to accommodate a route from Windsor Castle to the stadium.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 40 km was the historic distance. 21.0975 km is a half marathon.

questions.question: Which American swimmer is the most decorated Olympian of all time, with a total of 28 Olympic medals (including 23 golds)?
questions.explanation_correct: Michael Phelps competed in five Olympic games between 2000 and 2016, holding records for total medals and gold medals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Spitz won 7 golds in 1972. Thorpe is Australian. Dressel is a modern Olympic champion but has fewer medals.

questions.question: Which 1937 Disney release was the world's first full-length cel-animated feature film?
options: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.answer: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
questions.explanation_correct: Snow White was a massive commercial success, earning Walt Disney a custom honorary Academy Award.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pinocchio and Fantasia were released in 1940. Dumbo was released in 1941.

questions.question: Which American actor won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his role in 'Scent of a Woman' and starred in 'The Godfather' and 'Scarface'?
questions.explanation_correct: Al Pacino played Michael Corleone in 'The Godfather' and Tony Montana in 'Scarface', winning his Oscar for 'Scent of a Woman' (1992).
questions.explanation_incorrect: De Niro co-starred in Godfather Part II. Nicholson has three Oscars. Hoffman starred in 'Rain Man'.

questions.question: Which green-clad adventurer is the main playable protagonist in Nintendo's 'The Legend of Zelda' fantasy game series?
questions.explanation_correct: Link is the silent protagonist of the franchise, tasked with saving the kingdom of Hyrule and Princess Zelda.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zelda is the princess. Ganon is the antagonist. Mario is from another Nintendo franchise.

questions.question: Which HBO fantasy drama series, based on George R.R. Martin's novels, aired from 2011 to 2019 and featured Westeros?
options: Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power
questions.explanation_correct: Game of Thrones was a major television hit, focusing on noble families fighting for the Iron Throne of Westeros.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Witcher is on Netflix. House of the Dragon is a prequel. Rings of Power is on Amazon Prime.

questions.question: Which silent film won the first-ever Academy Award for Outstanding Picture at the inaugural ceremony in 1929?
options: Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans
questions.explanation_correct: Wings (1927), a romantic action film about WWI fighter pilots, remains the only silent film to win the top Oscar until 'The Artist' (2011).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sunrise won Unique and Artistic Picture. Metropolis was German. The Jazz Singer (first talkie) was disqualified from main competition.

questions.question: Which British rock band recorded the 1975 hit song 'Bohemian Rhapsody', written by lead singer Freddie Mercury?
questions.explanation_correct: Queen released 'Bohemian Rhapsody' on their album 'A Night at the Opera', featuring a famous operatic midsection.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other bands are prominent British rock acts but did not write this song.

questions.question: Which film series directed by Peter Jackson features 'The Fellowship of the Ring', 'The Two Towers', and 'The Return of the King'?
questions.explanation_correct: Peter Jackson shot the epic trilogy concurrently in New Zealand, winning 17 Academy Awards in total.
questions.explanation_incorrect: The Hobbit is a prequel trilogy. Narnia and Harry Potter are separate fantasy franchises.

questions.question: From which country does the famous pop group ABBA, known for hits like 'Dancing Queen' and 'Mamma Mia', originate?
questions.explanation_correct: ABBA formed in Stockholm, Sweden, in 1972, and became one of the most successful pop groups in history after winning Eurovision 1974.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other countries are also in Europe but are not ABBA's homeland.

questions.question: Which French scholar and philologist successfully deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone?
questions.explanation_correct: Champollion published his breakthrough in 1822, demonstrating that the hieroglyphic writing system was a combination of phonetic and ideographic signs.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Young made early contributions but didn't fully decode it. Lepsius was a later Egyptologist. Carter discovered Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922.

questions.question: Which treaty, signed in 843 AD, divided the vast Frankish Empire of Charlemagne among his three surviving grandsons?
questions.explanation_correct: The Treaty of Verdun ended a three-year civil war, dividing the empire into West Francia, East Francia, and Middle Francia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mersen (870) and Ribemont (880) further adjusted these borders. Aachen was the imperial capital and site of earlier accords.

questions.question: Which ruler became the first Emperor of a unified China in 221 BC, initiating the Qin dynasty and ordering the Terracotta Army?
questions.explanation_correct: Qin Shi Huang conquered all of the Warring States, unified China, standardized writing and currency, and began the Great Wall.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Han Wudi was a famous Han dynasty ruler. Kublai Khan was a Mongol ruler who founded the Yuan dynasty. Gaozu was the founder of the Han dynasty.

questions.question: What was the codename of the secret US research and development project that produced the first nuclear weapons during World War II?
questions.explanation_correct: The Manhattan Project was led by the United States with support from the UK and Canada, under the scientific direction of J. Robert Oppenheimer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Overlord was the Normandy invasion codename. Trinity was the codename of the first nuclear test in July 1945.

questions.question: Which Soviet space probe, launched in September 1959, was the first human-made object to reach the surface of the Moon?
questions.explanation_correct: Luna 2 successfully impacted the lunar surface on September 14, 1959, confirming that the Moon had no major magnetic field.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Luna 1 missed the Moon. Sputnik 1 was the first satellite. Vostok 1 was Yuri Gagarin's manned spacecraft.

questions.question: Which Portuguese explorer became the first European to reach India by sea, arriving in Calicut in 1498?
questions.explanation_correct: Vasco da Gama's voyage opened the sea route from Europe to Asia, establishing Portuguese dominance in the Indian Ocean.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Magellan led the first global circumnavigation. Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope first. Columbus sailed west to the Americas.

questions.question: Who was the principal author of the United States Declaration of Independence, adopted by the Continental Congress in 1776?
questions.explanation_correct: Thomas Jefferson drafted the document in Philadelphia, drawing on Enlightenment philosophy to declare the colonies' independence.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Franklin and Adams served on the drafting committee. Washington was leading the Continental Army and was not in the Congress.

questions.question: Which British king abdicated the throne in December 1936 to marry the American divorcée Wallis Simpson, causing a constitutional crisis?
questions.explanation_correct: Edward VIII abdicated after reigning for less than a year, and was succeeded by his younger brother, who became King George VI.
questions.explanation_incorrect: George V was his father. George VI was his brother. Edward VII was his grandfather, ruling from 1901 to 1910.

questions.question: Which river flows through the Grand Canyon in Arizona, serving as the primary agent of its erosion over millions of years?
questions.explanation_correct: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon, flowing 1,450 miles from the Rocky Mountains to the Gulf of California.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Mississippi is in the central US. Rio Grande forms the US-Mexico border. Columbia flows through the Pacific Northwest.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Switzerland, serving as the de facto seat of government?
questions.explanation_correct: Bern is the federal city (Bundesstadt) and capital of Switzerland, known for its well-preserved medieval city center.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Zurich is the largest city and financial center. Geneva is home to many international organizations. Basel is on the northern border.

questions.question: What is the largest desert in the world, covering an area of approximately 14 million square kilometers?
questions.explanation_correct: A desert is defined by low precipitation; Antarctica is a cold, polar desert and is the largest on Earth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sahara is the largest hot desert (~9 million km²). Arabian and Gobi are also large but smaller than Sahara.

questions.question: Which ancient, half-built, half-carved city in Jordan is famous for its rock-cut architecture and water conduit system?
questions.explanation_correct: Petra, established as the capital of the Nabataeans in the 4th century BC, is also known as the Rose City.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Palmyra is in Syria. Persepolis was in Persia. Ephesus is a classical Greek city in Turkey.

questions.question: What is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, separated from the Italian mainland by the Strait of Messina?
questions.explanation_correct: Sicily is an autonomous region of Italy, home to Mount Etna, and has an area of 25,711 square kilometers.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sardinia is the second largest. Cyprus is third. Crete is the fifth largest (largest in Greece).

questions.question: Which mountain range is traditionally considered the northern part of the boundary between the continents of Europe and Asia?
questions.explanation_correct: The Ural Mountains run from the Arctic Ocean down to Kazakhstan, dividing the Russian plains from Siberia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alps are in Western/Central Europe. Caucasus separates Europe and Asia in the south. Carpathians are in Eastern Europe.

questions.question: Which historic Italian city is famous for its network of 177 canals, 391 bridges, and lack of wheeled motor vehicles?
questions.explanation_correct: Venice (Venezia) is built on a group of 118 small islands in the Venetian Lagoon, with transport relying on boats and walking.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Florence is inland. Naples is a southern port. Genoa is a major northern port but has roads.

questions.question: Which river has the largest drainage basin and the largest water flow volume in the world, discharging more water than the next seven rivers combined?
questions.explanation_correct: The Amazon River has a massive flow and basin, accounting for approximately 20% of the world's total river flow.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nile is traditionally the longest. Yangtze is the longest in Asia. Congo is the deepest river in the world.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system has the most prominent and extensive planetary ring system, composed of water ice and rock?
questions.explanation_correct: Saturn's rings extend up to 120,700 km from the planet but are extremely thin, averaging only about 10 meters in thickness.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune have ring systems, but they are faint, dark, and far less extensive.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for the precious metal Gold, derived from its Latin name 'Aurum'?
questions.explanation_correct: The symbol Au represents Gold, which has an atomic number of 79 and is highly resistant to chemical corrosion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ag is Silver (Argentum). Gd is Gadolinium. Go is not a valid chemical symbol.

questions.question: What is the basic structural, functional, and biological unit of all known living organisms?
questions.explanation_correct: The cell is the smallest unit of life that can replicate independently, consisting of cytoplasm enclosed within a membrane.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Atom and Molecule are chemical units, not biological units of life. Organ is a collection of tissues.

questions.question: Which theoretical physicist formulated the special and general theories of relativity, reshaping modern physics in the early 20th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Albert Einstein published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1915, replacing Newtonian gravity with spacetime curvature.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Planck founded quantum theory. Bohr developed the atomic model. Heisenberg formulated the uncertainty principle.

questions.question: Which dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, discovered in 1930, was classified as the ninth planet of our solar system until its reclassification in 2006?
questions.explanation_correct: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006 after defining a planet as having 'cleared its orbit'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eris is another dwarf planet whose discovery triggered the debate. Ceres is in the asteroid belt. Makemake is in the Kuiper belt.

questions.question: What is the name of the green pigment found in plants that absorbs light energy for use in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation_correct: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light while reflecting green light, allowing plants to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Carotenoids are yellow/orange pigments. Anthocyanins are red/purple. Hemoglobin is the iron-containing oxygen transport protein in blood.

questions.question: Which chemical element, represented by the symbol He, is the second lightest and second most abundant in the observable universe?
questions.explanation_correct: Helium is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, non-toxic, and inert noble gas that is primarily produced by stellar nuclear fusion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hydrogen is the lightest. Lithium is the third lightest. Neon is a heavier noble gas.

questions.question: What is the SI derived unit of force, named after the scientist who formulated the laws of classical mechanics?
questions.explanation_correct: One Newton (N) is defined as the force needed to accelerate a one-kilogram mass at a rate of one meter per second squared.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Joule is for energy. Pascal is for pressure. Watt is for power.

questions.question: Which Spanish Surrealist painter created 'The Persistence of Memory' in 1931, featuring melting pocket watches?
questions.explanation_correct: Dalí's painting uses bizarre imagery to evoke dream-like states, featuring the soft, melting watches on a desolate landscape.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Picasso was cubist. Miró had abstract surrealist style. Magritte was a Belgian surrealist.

questions.question: Which English author and academic wrote the fantasy novel 'The Hobbit' (1937) and the epic trilogy 'The Lord of the Rings'?
questions.explanation_correct: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, creating Middle-earth and its languages.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lewis wrote Narnia. Orwell wrote 1984. Rowling wrote Harry Potter.

questions.question: Which Austrian musical prodigy and composer wrote iconic works like 'The Magic Flute' and 'Don Giovanni' before dying at age 35?
questions.explanation_correct: Mozart composed over 600 works, displaying extraordinary talent from early childhood in keyboard and violin.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Beethoven died at 56. Haydn was a mentor who died at 77. Schubert died at 31.

questions.question: Which French sculptor designed the copper statue of Liberty Enlightening the World, dedicated in New York Harbor in 1886?
questions.explanation_correct: Bartholdi sculpted the Statue of Liberty, while the internal structural framework was engineered by Gustave Eiffel.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Eiffel was the structural engineer. Rodin and Carpeaux were other famous French sculptors.

questions.question: Which English novelist and essayist wrote the dystopian novel 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' and the allegorical novella 'Animal Farm'?
questions.explanation_correct: George Orwell (pen name of Eric Arthur Blair) wrote these works criticizing totalitarianism and political manipulation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Huxley wrote 'Brave New World'. Wells wrote 'The Time Machine'. Woolf was a modernist pioneer.

questions.question: Which 20th-century avant-garde art movement sought to release the creative potential of the unconscious mind, often through dream imagery?
questions.explanation_correct: Surrealism, founded by André Breton in Paris in 1924, was heavily influenced by psychoanalysis and Freud's dream theories.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cubism broke down objects. Dadaism was anti-art. Fauvism used wild, unnatural colors.

questions.question: Which massive oval amphitheater in the center of Rome was built under the Flavian emperors Vespasian and Titus in the 1st century AD?
questions.explanation_correct: The Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheater) could hold up to 80,000 spectators for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pantheon is a temple with a dome. Circus Maximus was for chariot racing. Forum Romanum was the political center.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock in 399 BC for 'corrupting the youth' of Athens?
questions.explanation_correct: Socrates left no writings, but his conversational method of inquiry was documented by his student Plato.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Plato, Aristotle, and Diogenes died of natural causes in later decades.

questions.question: Which legendary Brazilian footballer, who died in 2022, is the only player in history to win three FIFA World Cups?
questions.explanation_correct: Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento) won the World Cup in 1958, 1962, and 1970, and scored over 1,200 career goals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Maradona won one World Cup (1986). Ronaldo won two (1994, 2002). Garrincha won two (1958, 1962).

questions.question: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is held annually in Paris, France, on clay courts, and is named after a French aviator?
questions.explanation_correct: The French Open (commonly known as Roland Garros) is the only clay-court Grand Slam, demanding great physical endurance.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other options are played on grass or hard courts.

questions.question: How often are the summer and winter Olympic Games held respectively, excluding cancellations or delays?
questions.explanation_correct: The Olympic games are held every four years, with summer and winter games alternating every two years.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other intervals are historically incorrect.

questions.question: How many players are on the court for a single team during a standard regulation basketball game?
questions.explanation_correct: A basketball team has 5 active players on the court: usually two guards, two forwards, and a center.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other numbers are typical for other versions of the sport (e.g., 3-on-3) or different sports.

questions.question: What is the name of the vulcanized rubber disc used in ice hockey instead of a ball?
questions.explanation_correct: A hockey puck is 1 inch thick, 3 inches in diameter, and is frozen before games to reduce bouncing.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other terms are simply descriptive or incorrect.

questions.question: Which country is home to the historic Autodromo Nazionale Monza, famous for hosting the Formula One Italian Grand Prix?
questions.explanation_correct: Monza is located north of Milan, Italy, and is known as the Temple of Speed due to its long straights.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monaco hosts the street circuit. France and Spain host races on other tracks (Paul Ricard, Barcelona).

questions.question: How many hurdles must a runner clear in a standard Olympic 400 meters hurdles race?
questions.explanation_correct: Both men's and women's 400m hurdles races feature exactly 10 hurdles spaced evenly around the track.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other counts are incorrect for the 400m distance.

questions.question: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football, excluding any subsequent extra points or conversions?
questions.explanation_correct: A touchdown is worth 6 points, after which the scoring team can attempt an extra point (1 point) or two-point conversion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 3 points is for a field goal. 7 is the common total after a successful extra point. 2 points is for a safety or conversion.

questions.question: Which American heavyweight boxer, born Cassius Clay, is widely considered one of the greatest athletes of the 20th century?
questions.explanation_correct: Muhammad Ali was a three-time world heavyweight champion and an activist, famous for his 'float like a butterfly, sting like a bee' style.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Frazier was his famous rival. Tyson was champion in the 80s/90s. Leonard was a middleweight champion.

questions.question: Which British-American film director is known for directing the blockbusters 'Inception', 'Interstellar', and 'Oppenheimer'?
questions.explanation_correct: Christopher Nolan is celebrated for his complex storytelling, practical effects, and won Best Director for 'Oppenheimer' (2023).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tarantino directed 'Pulp Fiction'. Villeneuve directed 'Dune'. Cameron directed 'Avatar' and 'Titanic'.

questions.question: Which media franchise, focusing on collectible creatures and starring Pikachu, is the highest-grossing media franchise of all time?
questions.explanation_correct: Pokémon, created by Satoshi Tajiri in 1996 for Nintendo, has generated over $100 billion in revenue across games, cards, and merchandise.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hello Kitty is second. Star Wars is fifth. MCU is further down.

questions.question: Which American subscription streaming service produced the hit series 'Stranger Things', 'Squid Game', and 'The Crown'?
questions.explanation_correct: Netflix pioneered streaming media, investing heavily in original programming and gaining over 260 million subscribers worldwide.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Prime Video produced 'The Boys'. Disney+ has Star Wars and Marvel. HBO Max is known for 'Succession'.

questions.question: Which fictional British secret service agent was created by writer Ian Fleming in 1953, starring in 25 Eon Productions films?
questions.explanation_correct: James Bond (Agent 007) has been portrayed by six actors in the official film franchise, starting with Sean Connery in 1962.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bourne was created by Robert Ludlum. Hunt is the protagonist of Mission: Impossible. Jack Ryan was created by Tom Clancy.

questions.question: Which American singer, songwriter, and actress is widely known as the 'Queen of Pop', releasing hits like 'Like a Virgin' and 'Vogue'?
questions.explanation_correct: Madonna is the best-selling female recording artist of all time, famous for her continuous reinvention and provocative work.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Whitney Houston was a legendary vocalist. Lady Gaga and Cher are prominent icons but are not the 'Queen of Pop'.

questions.question: Which animation studio, founded in 1986 and owned by Disney, produced the first-ever feature-length computer-animated film, 'Toy Story'?
questions.explanation_correct: Pixar Animation Studios revolutionized the animation industry, releasing 'Toy Story' in 1995 and winning numerous Academy Awards.
questions.explanation_incorrect: DreamWorks made 'Shrek'. Ghibli is Japanese hand-drawn. Illumination made 'Despicable Me'.

questions.question: What is the real name of the wealthy industrialist who fights crime as the vigilante Batman in DC Comics?
questions.explanation_correct: Bruce Wayne witnessed the murder of his parents in Gotham City, leading him to train and adopt the bat persona.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Clark Kent is Superman. Peter Parker is Spider-Man. Tony Stark is Iron Man.

questions.question: Which English rock band released the iconic 1969 album 'Abbey Road', featuring a cover showing them crossing a zebra walk?
questions.explanation_correct: The Beatles recorded 'Abbey Road' as their last joint studio project, featuring classic tracks like 'Something' and 'Here Comes the Sun'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other bands are contemporary British invasion rock bands but did not record this album.

questions.question: Which Jamaican singer-songwriter and musician is widely regarded as a pioneer of reggae, releasing hits like 'One Love'?
questions.explanation_correct: Bob Marley and the Wailers popularized reggae music globally, combining spiritual Rastafari themes with political messages.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cliff and Tosh were other reggae pioneers. Shaggy is a modern dancehall artist.

questions.question: Which river did Julius Caesar cross with his legion in 49 BC, committing treason and sparking a Roman civil war?
questions.explanation_correct: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon river in northern Italy breached Roman law, leading to his famous phrase 'alea iacta est' (the die is cast).
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tiber flows through Rome. Po is Italy's longest river. Rhine was the northern border of Roman expansion.

questions.question: Which French city was besieged by the English in 1428, only to be famously relieved by Joan of Arc in 1429?
questions.explanation_correct: The lifting of the Siege of Orléans was Joan of Arc's first major military victory and a turning point in the Hundred Years' War.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Rouen was where Joan was executed. Reims was where Charles VII was crowned. Paris was under Anglo-Burgundian control.

questions.question: Which military alliance of Soviet bloc countries was established in 1955 in response to West Germany joining NATO?
questions.explanation_correct: The Warsaw Pact (Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance) was signed in Warsaw and led by the Soviet Union.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Comecon was the economic organization. Iron Curtain was a political barrier concept. Non-Aligned Movement was for neutral states.

questions.question: Which empire issued the infamous 'blank check' of unconditional support to Austria-Hungary in July 1914, escalating the crisis?
questions.explanation_correct: Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany assured Austria-Hungary that Germany would support whatever action it took against Serbia.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Russia supported Serbia. Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers later. Britain sought to mediate before declaring war.

questions.question: Which war, lasting from 1950 to 1953, ended with an armistice establishing a demilitarized zone near the 38th parallel?
questions.explanation_correct: The Korean War began with North Korea's invasion of South Korea, leading to a UN-backed coalition fighting Chinese and North Korean forces.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Vietnam War ended in 1975. Suez Crisis occurred in 1956. Soviet-Afghan War lasted from 1979 to 1889.

questions.question: Which Italian navigator mapped the South American coast between 1497 and 1504, demonstrating it was a new continent and not Asia?
questions.explanation_correct: German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller named the new continents 'America' in 1507, using a feminized Latin version of Vespucci's first name.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cabot explored North America. Verrazzano mapped the Atlantic coast. Columbus insisted he had reached outer parts of Asia.

questions.question: Who was the last Emperor of Russia, abdicating in 1917 and executed with his family by Bolsheviks in 1918?
questions.explanation_correct: Nicholas II of the Romanov dynasty abdicated during the February Revolution, ending over three centuries of Romanov rule.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Alexander III was his father. Nicholas I ruled during the Crimean War. Alexander II freed the serfs and was assassinated in 1881.

questions.question: Which English weaver and carpenter invented the multi-spindle spinning frame, known as the 'spinning jenny', in 1764?
questions.explanation_correct: James Hargreaves' spinning jenny allowed a single worker to spin multiple spools of thread at once, accelerating yarn production.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Arkwright patented the water frame. Crompton invented the spinning mule. Whitney invented the cotton gin.

questions.question: What is the name of the ocean that completely surrounds the continent of Antarctica, officially recognized by the IHO in 2000?
questions.explanation_correct: The Southern Ocean (Antarctic Ocean) comprises the southernmost waters of the World Ocean, bounded by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other oceans border the Southern Ocean but do not extend all the way to the Antarctic coast.

questions.question: What is the capital and most populous city of Japan, forming the world's most populous metropolitan area?
questions.explanation_correct: Tokyo (formerly Edo) became the capital when Emperor Meiji moved his seat there from Kyoto in 1869.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kyoto was the historic imperial capital. Osaka and Yokohama are major cities but are not the capital.

questions.question: Which major mountain range in Asia contains all of the world's 14 peaks that rise above 8,000 meters?
questions.explanation_correct: The Himalayas contain Mount Everest, K2, and 12 other 'eight-thousanders', forming a barrier between the Indian subcontinent and Tibet.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Andes are in South America. Rockies are in North America. Alps are in Europe. None of these have peaks near 8,000m.

questions.question: What is the indigenous Pitjantjatjara name for the massive sandstone monolith in central Australia, historically known as Ayers Rock?
questions.explanation_correct: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people, and ownership was formally returned to them in 1985.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kata Tjuta is a nearby rock formation. Kakadu is a national park in the north. Purnululu contains the Bungle Bungle Range.

questions.question: Which island country in the Indian Ocean, located off the southeastern coast of Africa, is the fourth-largest island in the world?
questions.explanation_correct: Madagascar split from the Indian landmass 88 million years ago, allowing its flora and fauna to evolve in relative isolation.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Sri Lanka is off India. Mauritius and Seychelles are small island nations.

questions.question: What is the name of the cold desert that covers parts of northern and northwestern China and southern Mongolia?
questions.explanation_correct: The Gobi Desert is a rain shadow desert formed by the Himalayas blocking rain-bearing clouds, known for its extreme temperature swings.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Taklamakan is in western China. Karakum is in Turkmenistan. Thar is in northwestern India and Pakistan.

questions.question: Which sovereign state is the smallest in the world by both area and population, completely enclaved within Rome, Italy?
questions.explanation_correct: Vatican City covers just 49 hectares (121 acres) and was established as an independent state by the Lateran Treaty in 1929.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Monaco is the second smallest. San Marino is third. Liechtenstein is in central Europe, not enclaved in Rome.

questions.question: Which river, along with the Euphrates, forms the major river system of Mesopotamia, flowing through Baghdad, Iraq?
questions.explanation_correct: The Tigris flows 1,150 miles from Turkey through Iraq, joining the Euphrates to form the Shatt al-Arab waterway.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Nile is in Egypt. Jordan flows into the Dead Sea. Indus flows through Pakistan.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system features the Great Red Spot, a massive persistent anticyclonic storm larger than Earth?
questions.explanation_correct: Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been observed for over 150 years and features wind speeds up to 432 km/h.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Saturn has seasonal storms. Mars is a rocky planet. Neptune has the Great Dark Spot, which is smaller and transient.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for Oxygen, which is the second-most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation_correct: Oxygen has the atomic number 8 and symbol O, playing a crucial role in cellular respiration and combustion.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Ox, Og (Oganesson), and Op are not the chemical symbols for oxygen.

questions.question: What is the name of the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize nutrients from carbon dioxide and water?
questions.explanation_correct: Photosynthesis converts solar energy into chemical energy, producing oxygen as a byproduct.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose. Transpiration is water movement. Fermentation is anaerobic energy production.

questions.question: Which stable subatomic particle carries a single negative elementary electric charge and orbits the atomic nucleus?
questions.explanation_correct: Electrons have a tiny mass and orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels, determining the chemical properties of atoms.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Protons are positive and in the nucleus. Neutrons are neutral. Positrons are positive antimatter equivalents.

questions.question: What is the name of the brightest star in the night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major and also known as the 'Dog Star'?
questions.explanation_correct: Sirius (Sirius A) is highly visible due to its proximity to Earth (8.6 light-years) and its high intrinsic luminosity.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant. Polaris is the North Star. Alpha Centauri is the closest star system.

questions.question: What is the historically accepted average normal temperature of the human body in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation_correct: 37 °C (98.6 °F) was established as average normal temperature by Carl Wunderlich in the 19th century, though individuals vary.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other values represent mild hypothermia or low-grade fever.

questions.question: What carbon-based mineral is the hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth, scoring a 10 on the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.explanation_correct: Diamonds have a rigid giant covalent structure of carbon atoms, giving them exceptional hardness.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Graphite is soft carbon. Quartz is silica (7 on Mohs). Corundum is sapphire/ruby material (9 on Mohs).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of frequency, defined as one cycle per second?
questions.explanation_correct: The Hertz (Hz), named after Heinrich Hertz, is used to measure periodic phenomena like sound waves and radio signals.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tesla measures magnetic field. Weber measures magnetic flux. Becquerel measures radioactive decay.

questions.question: Which Italian Early Renaissance painter created the masterpieces 'The Birth of Venus' and 'Primavera'?
questions.explanation_correct: Botticelli painted 'The Birth of Venus' in the mid-1480s, depicting the goddess Venus emerging from the sea on a shell.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Da Vinci and Raphael were High Renaissance. Lippi was Botticelli's teacher.

questions.question: Which American author wrote the classic 1851 novel 'Moby-Dick', detailing Captain Ahab's obsessive quest for a white whale?
questions.explanation_correct: Melville's epic explores themes of class, social status, good and evil, drawing on his own whaling experiences.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Hawthorne wrote 'The Scarlet Letter'. Poe wrote gothic fiction. Twain wrote 'Huckleberry Finn'.

questions.question: Which German-British Baroque composer wrote the famous 1741 English oratorio 'Messiah', containing the 'Hallelujah' chorus?
questions.explanation_correct: Handel composed 'Messiah' in London in just 24 days, and it remains one of the most performed choral works in Western music.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Bach was German. Vivaldi was Italian. Purcell was an earlier English composer.

questions.question: Which ancient Hellenistic Greek marble sculpture, discovered on a Mediterranean island in 1863, depicts a winged goddess of victory?
questions.explanation_correct: The Winged Victory (Nike of Samothrace) is displayed at the top of the Daru staircase in the Louvre Museum.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Venus de Milo is another Louvre masterpiece but is wingless. Laocoön is in Rome. Discobolus is by Myron.

questions.question: Which Russian novelist wrote the massive realist epic 'War and Peace' (1869), detailing the French invasion of Russia?
questions.explanation_correct: Tolstoy's masterpiece blends fictional narratives with historical philosophy, tracking five aristocratic families.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Dostoevsky wrote 'Crime and Punishment'. Chekhov was a playwright. Turgenev wrote 'Fathers and Sons'.

questions.question: Which early 20th-century avant-garde art movement, pioneered by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, revolutionized painting by using geometric shapes?
questions.explanation_correct: Cubism abandoned traditional perspective, depicting subjects from multiple angles simultaneously using interlocking planes.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Surrealism focused on dreams. Expressionism on emotion. Futurism on speed and technology.

questions.question: Which historic circular temple in Rome features a massive concrete dome with a central opening (oculus) open to the sky?
questions.explanation_correct: Completed under Hadrian around 126 AD, the Pantheon's dome remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Colosseum is an oval amphitheater. Temple of Vesta is a small circular shrine. Basilica of Maxentius was a civic building.

questions.question: Which German philosopher wrote 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' and introduced the concept of the Übermensch (Overman)?
questions.explanation_correct: Nietzsche's work critiqued traditional morality and religion, emphasizing the 'will to power' and individual greatness.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Schopenhauer wrote on pessimism. Kant formulated transcendental idealism. Marx founded historical materialism.

questions.question: In which Swiss city is the international headquarters of FIFA (Federation Internationale de Football Association) located?
questions.explanation_correct: FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904 but moved its headquarters to Zurich in 1932.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Geneva hosts other organizations. Lausanne is home to the IOC. Nyon is the headquarters of UEFA.

questions.question: On which type of court surface are both the US Open and Australian Open Grand Slam tournaments played?
questions.explanation_correct: Both tournaments use acrylic-topped hard court surfaces, offering a medium-fast speed of play.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Clay is for French Open. Grass is for Wimbledon. Carpet is no longer used in professional tours.

questions.question: Near which ancient Greek sanctuary of Zeus were the original Olympic Games held from 776 BC to 393 AD?
questions.explanation_correct: The ancient games were held at Olympia every four years, featuring athletic contests among various city-states.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Athens hosted the first modern games. Delphi hosted the Pythian Games. Sparta was a competitor.

questions.question: What is the official inside diameter of a standard NBA basketball rim in inches?
questions.explanation_correct: All standard basketball rims have an inside diameter of 18 inches (45.72 cm), twice the size of a standard basketball.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other measurements do not comply with official basketball rules.

questions.question: How many players are on the ice for a single team, including the goaltender, during standard play in ice hockey?
questions.explanation_correct: A standard ice hockey lineup on the ice consists of a goaltender, two defensemen, and three forwards.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 5 is the number of skaters excluding the goalie. 7 and 11 are for other sports.

questions.question: What was the nationality of Ayrton Senna, the legendary three-time Formula One World Champion who died in a crash in 1994?
questions.explanation_correct: Ayrton Senna was born in São Paulo, Brazil, and became one of the country's greatest national sports icons.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Other nationalities are incorrect; Senna was proud of his Brazilian heritage.

questions.question: How many individual track and field events are contested in a standard men's Olympic decathlon?
questions.explanation_correct: The decathlon (from Greek 'deca' meaning ten) is held over two days, testing a combination of speed, strength, and endurance.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 7 is for the heptathlon (usually women). 8 and 12 are not standard Olympic multi-event counts.

questions.question: How many points is a successful field goal worth in American football?
questions.explanation_correct: A field goal is scored by kicking the ball through the opponent's goalposts from the field, earning 3 points.
questions.explanation_incorrect: 1 point is for a conversion kick. 6 is for a touchdown. 2 points is for a safety or conversion run.

questions.question: Which controversial American heavyweight champion was disqualified in 1997 for biting off a piece of Evander Holyfield's ear?
questions.explanation_correct: Mike Tyson bit Holyfield's ears twice during their rematch in Las Vegas, leading to his disqualification and license suspension.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Lewis and Bowe were other champions. Holyfield was the victim of the bite.

questions.question: Which English film director is widely regarded as the 'Master of Suspense', famous for directing 'Psycho' and 'The Birds'?
questions.explanation_correct: Hitchcock pioneered many techniques in the suspense and psychological thriller genres, directing over 50 films.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Kubrick directed 'The Shining'. Welles directed 'Citizen Kane'. Wilder directed 'Some Like It Hot'.

questions.question: Which bounty hunter, wearing a powered suit, serves as the main protagonist of Nintendo's 'Metroid' science fiction series?
questions.explanation_correct: Samus Aran was revealed as a woman at the end of the original 1986 game, making her one of the first major female game protagonists.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Peach is from Mario. Fox is from Star Fox. Captain Falcon is from F-Zero.

questions.question: What is the name of the high school chemistry teacher who turns to producing methamphetamine in the TV drama 'Breaking Bad'?
questions.explanation_correct: Walter White (portrayed by Bryan Cranston) adopts the alias 'Heisenberg' after being diagnosed with lung cancer.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Jesse Pinkman is his partner. Saul Goodman is their lawyer. Hank Schrader is his DEA agent brother-in-law.

questions.question: Which adventure film franchise, starring Harrison Ford, features 'Raiders of the Lost Ark' and 'The Last Crusade'?
questions.explanation_correct: Created by George Lucas and directed by Steven Spielberg, the franchise follows archaeologist Dr. Indiana Jones.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Tomb Raider stars Lara Croft. National Treasure stars Nicolas Cage. The Mummy is a separate franchise.

questions.question: Which British singer-songwriter released the massively successful albums '21' and '25', featuring hits like 'Hello'?
questions.explanation_correct: Adele's albums '21' (2011) and '25' (2015) earned her multiple Grammy Awards and are among the best-selling albums of the 21st century.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Winehouse sang 'Rehab'. Ed Sheeran has numeric titles (+, x, etc.). Dua Lipa is a dance-pop singer.

questions.question: What is the name of the fictional British school of magic attended by Harry Potter, Ron Weasley, and Hermione Granger?
questions.explanation_correct: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry is located in the Scottish Highlands and is the primary setting of the Harry Potter novels.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Beauxbatons and Durmstrang are other European magic schools. Ilvermorny is the North American magic school.

questions.question: Which DC Comics superhero is widely referred to as the 'Man of Steel' and was born on the planet Krypton as Kal-El?
questions.explanation_correct: Superman (Clark Kent) was created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster in 1938, serving as the archetype of the modern superhero.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Iron Man is from Marvel. Batman is the Caped Crusader. Cyborg is another DC hero but is half-robot.

questions.question: Which British-American rock band released the critically acclaimed 1977 album 'Rumours', which sold over 40 million copies?
questions.explanation_correct: Fleetwood Mac recorded 'Rumours' amidst intense personal relationships and breakups among band members, fueling its emotional depth.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Pink Floyd released 'Animals' in 1977. The Eagles released 'Hotel California' in late 1976.

questions.question: Which Swedish DJ and music producer, who died in 2018, recorded the global electronic hits 'Levels' and 'Wake Me Up'?
questions.explanation_correct: Avicii (Tim Bergling) was a pioneer of the EDM movement, combining country music elements with house music in 'Wake Me Up'.
questions.explanation_incorrect: Swedish House Mafia is a trio. Guetta is French. Kygo is Norwegian.
